Introduction

Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is the most abundant immunoglobulin in human serum (≈75–80% of total serum Ig; 8–16 mg/mL). It is the principal antibody of the secondary immune response — produced by plasma cells after class switching from IgM. IgG is the smallest antibody (monomer, 150 kDa), enabling excellent tissue penetration. It crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the neonate for the first 6 months of life.

Structure (3 marks)

  • Basic Y-shaped monomer — two identical heavy chains (γ, 50 kDa each) + two identical light chains (κ or λ, 25 kDa each), linked by disulfide bonds & non-covalent interactions.
  • Heavy chain (γ) — composed of 4 domains: VH (variable) + Cγ1, Cγ2, Cγ3 (constant). The Cγ2 domain carries the hinge-region & complement (C1q) binding site; Cγ3 binds Fc receptors (FcγR) on phagocytes.
  • Light chain — VL + CL.
  • Hinge region — flexible proline-rich segment between Cγ1 and Cγ2; allows Fab arms to open and bind epitopes at variable distances; susceptible to papain & pepsin cleavage.
  • Enzymatic cleavage
    • Papain — cleaves above hinge → 2 Fab fragments (antigen-binding, monovalent) + 1 Fc fragment (crystallisable; carries effector functions).
    • Pepsin — cleaves below hinge → 1 F(ab')₂ fragment (bivalent, can precipitate antigen) + small pFc' fragments.
  • Domains — Fab (Fragment antigen binding) at N-terminal end (VH + VL) — three hypervariable complementarity-determining regions (CDR1–3) form the paratope that binds the epitope; Fc (Fragment crystallisable) at C-terminal — mediates biological effector functions.
  • Carbohydrate moiety — N-linked oligosaccharide at Asn297 of Cγ2 — stabilises Fc structure & influences FcγR binding.
  • Subclasses (4) — IgG1 (66%), IgG2 (23%), IgG3 (7%), IgG4 (4%) — differ in hinge length, disulfide bonds, and biological function:
    • IgG1, IgG3 — strong complement activators; FcγR binding; protein antigens; respond to viruses, vaccines.
    • IgG2 — polysaccharide antigens (encapsulated bacteria — pneumococcus, Hib); weak complement activator.
    • IgG3 — strongest complement activation; shortest half-life (7 d); Rh antibodies.
    • IgG4 — weak complement; non-inflammatory; chronic antigen exposure (allergen immunotherapy); IgG4-related disease.
  • Half-life — ~21 days (longest of all Igs; due to FcRn-mediated recycling).

Functions (3 marks)

  1. Neutralisation — binds viral/bacterial surface antigens or toxins, blocking their attachment to host cell receptors (e.g., antitoxin IgG against tetanus, diphtheria; antiviral IgG against HBsAg).
  2. Opsonisation — IgG (especially IgG1, IgG3) coats microbes; Fc portion binds FcγRI (CD64) & FcγRII (CD32) on macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells → enhanced phagocytosis (≈1000-fold increase).
  3. Complement activation (classical pathway) — C1q binds Fc of IgG (requires ≥2 adjacent IgG molecules; IgM is more efficient); IgG3 > IgG1 > IgG2 >> IgG4.
  4. Antibody-Dependent Cell-mediated Cytotoxicity (ADCC) — IgG coats virus-infected/tumour cells; FcγRIII (CD16) on NK cells binds Fc → NK cell degranulation (perforin, granzyme) → target cell apoptosis.
  5. Transplacental transfer — FcRn (neonatal Fc receptor) in placental syncytiotrophoblast binds Fc of IgG (not other isotypes) → active transport to fetal circulation; provides passive immunity from ~20 weeks gestation, peaking at term.
  6. Half-life extension — FcRn in endothelial cells & monocytes recycles IgG, protecting from lysosomal degradation → 21-day half-life (basis for therapeutic monoclonal antibodies & IVIG therapy).
  7. Immune complex clearance — IgG-antigen complexes bind RBC complement receptors (CR1); transported to liver/spleen for phagocytosis.
  8. Feedback inhibition — IgG-antigen complex binds FcγRIIb on B cells → inhibits further B cell activation (immune complex feedback).
  9. Mucosal immunity (minor) — small amounts of IgG in mucosal secretions; IgA dominates.

Clinical Significance

  • Maternal IgG protects neonate for 6 months.
  • Used as therapeutic IVIG for immunodeficiency, ITP, Guillain-Barré, Kawasaki, autoimmune disease.
  • Subclass deficiency — recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated bacteria (IgG2 deficiency in children).
  • Hyper-IgG4 disease — IgG4-related disease (autoimmune pancreatitis, Mikulicz syndrome, Riedel thyroiditis).

Clinical Pearl

IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta — mediated by FcRn (Brambell receptor), which binds IgG in acidic endosomes (pH 6.5) and releases at physiological pH (7.4) on the fetal side. This explains why maternal IgG anti-D (Rh) causes haemolytic disease of the newborn — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses to fetal circulation and destroys Rh+ fetal RBCs. The same mechanism is exploited therapeutically: anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) given to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks & within 72 h of delivery clears fetal Rh+ cells before maternal B cells are sensitised. Also, because IgG has the longest half-life (21 d), it is the basis for monoclonal antibody therapy (trastuzumab, rituximab, infliximab) and for IVIG replacement therapy in primary immunodeficiency (400–600 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks).

Introduction

When bacteria are inoculated into a closed (batch) liquid culture medium under optimal conditions, they exhibit a characteristic growth curve with four phases: Lag, Log (Exponential), Stationary, and Decline (Death). Each phase is associated with distinct morphological, physiological, biochemical, and antigenic changes that have direct implications for laboratory diagnosis, antibiotic susceptibility, and vaccine production.

The Bacterial Growth Curve — Phases & Characteristics

1. Lag Phase (1–4 hours)

  • Definition — interval between inoculation and onset of active division. Bacteria adapt to new environment (synthesise enzymes, ribosomes, metabolites); no increase in cell number, but cells enlarge metabolically.
  • Morphology — cells are larger, more Gram-reactive, metabolically very active.
  • Biochemistry — increased RNA & protein synthesis; induced enzymes produced; high metabolic rate.
  • Antibiotic susceptibility — resistant to cell-wall antibiotics (penicillin, β-lactams) because cells are not actively dividing; sensitive to protein synthesis inhibitors.
  • Antigenicity — surface antigens (flagella, pili) being synthesised; poor antigen production.
  • Clinical relevance — bacteria in lag phase may give false-negative cultures or low antibiotic susceptibility results.

2. Logarithmic (Log / Exponential) Phase (4–8 hours)

  • Definition — period of maximal, constant division rate. Cells divide by binary fission at a constant rate (e.g., E. coli every 20 min, M. tuberculosis every 18–24 h).
  • Morphology — cells are smallest, uniform in size & shape, most Gram-reactive.
  • Biochemistry — maximum metabolic rate; balanced growth (DNA, RNA, protein, peptidoglycan all synthesised proportionally); most sensitive to antibiotics that target dividing cells.
  • Antibiotic susceptibility — maximum susceptibility to cell-wall inhibitors (penicillin, cephalosporin, vancomycin) — because peptidoglycan is actively being synthesised; also to fluoroquinolones (DNA replication), metronidazole (requires rapid metabolism). In vitro antibiotic susceptibility testing uses log-phase cultures.
  • Antigenicity — maximum antigen production; flagella, pili, capsules, exotoxins all at peak — ideal phase for vaccine preparation (e.g., acellular pertussis antigens, tetanus toxin harvested at log phase for toxoid vaccine).
  • Toxin production — maximum exotoxin production (e.g., tetanospasmin, diphtheria toxin, botulinum toxin).
  • Gram staining — most uniform staining; morphological identification best at this phase.
  • Phage susceptibility — maximum — log-phase cultures used for phage typing.

3. Stationary Phase (8–24 hours)

  • Definition — equilibrium between cell division and cell death; growth rate equals death rate. Caused by nutrient depletion, accumulation of toxic waste products (acids, H₂O₂), oxygen depletion.
  • Morphology — cells are smaller (dwarf forms), pleomorphic, irregular in staining (Gram-variable).
  • Biochemistry — shift to secondary metabolism; sporulation begins in spore-formers (Bacillus, Clostridium); pigments produced (e.g., pyocyanin in Pseudomonas, prodigiosin in Serratia); antibiotics produced (e.g., streptomycin from S. griseus, penicillin from P. chrysogenum).
  • Antibiotic susceptibility — reduced; cells are not actively dividing → β-lactams ineffective. Persisters (dormant cells) develop — tolerance phenotype.
  • Antigenicity — capsular antigens, spore antigens appear.
  • Intracellular inclusions — granules (volutin/metachromatic granules in C. diphtheriae; poly-β-hydroxybutyrate; glycogen).
  • Clinical relevance — chronic infections (e.g., TB) often have stationary-phase bacteria; explains antibiotic tolerance in biofilms.

4. Decline / Death Phase (after 24 hours)

  • Definition — exponential decline in viable cell count; exceeds new cell formation. Death due to nutrient exhaustion, toxic byproducts, autolysis.
  • Morphology — involution forms (abnormal, bizarre shapes); massive pleomorphism; Gram-negative staining (loss of cell wall integrity); ghost cells.
  • Biochemistry — autolysins activated; release of intracellular contents.
  • Antibiotic susceptibility — minimal; viable but non-culturable (VBNC) state.
  • Clinical relevance — old cultures give misleading Gram stain & morphology; subculture to fresh medium before identification.

Clinical Pearl

The log phase is critical for antibiotic susceptibility testing — this is why the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method uses a 0.5 McFarland turbidity standard (≈1.5 × 10⁸ CFU/mL) prepared from a fresh 18–24 h culture, then applied to Mueller-Hinton agar within 15 min to ensure log-phase growth. β-lactam antibiotics (penicillin, cephalosporin) only kill actively dividing cells because they target peptidoglycan cross-linking during cell wall synthesis — this is the basis of "time-dependent killing" and why chronic biofilm infections (stationary phase) are refractory to β-lactams. Conversely, aminoglycosides (gentamicin) require active transport into the cell (oxygen-dependent) — they are ineffective against anaerobes and biofilm bacteria. Persister cells (a small subpopulation in stationary phase that enter dormancy) are now recognised as the cause of recurrent infections (e.g., TB, UTI) — they survive antibiotic exposure without genetic resistance and resuscitate when the antibiotic is withdrawn.

Introduction

Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with chitin-containing cell walls, ergosterol-containing cell membranes, and a heterotrophic (absorptive) mode of nutrition. They are classified morphologically into four broad groups: yeasts, yeast-like fungi, moulds (filamentous fungi), and dimorphic fungi. This morphological classification is clinically useful because it correlates with the type of infection and the laboratory identification approach.

Morphological Classification

1. Yeasts (1 mark)

  • Morphology — unicellular; round or oval cells (3–8 µm); reproduce asexually by budding (blastogenesis) — daughter cell pinches off from mother. Some form pseudohyphae (chains of elongated yeast cells that don't fully separate, with constrictions at septa).
  • Colony on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) — creamy, pasty, bacteria-like colonies.
  • Examples
    • Candida albicans — opportunistic; oral thrush, vulvovaginitis, disseminated candidiasis; forms germ tube at 37 °C in serum.
    • Cryptococcus neoformans — encapsulated yeast; meningitis in HIV/AIDS; India ink stain shows clear halo; urease positive.
    • Saccharomyces cerevisiae — baker's/brewer's yeast; rarely pathogenic.
    • Malassezia furfur — lipophilic yeast; pityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis; "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on KOH mount.
    • Trichosporon — white piedra; invasive in immunocompromised.
    • Rhodotorula — red colonies; catheter-related infection.

2. Yeast-like Fungi (½ mark)

  • Morphology — intermediate between yeast and mould; grow as yeast at 37 °C but form pseudohyphae (chains of yeast cells with constrictions) at lower temperatures or under certain conditions.
  • Examples
    • Candida albicans (also classified as yeast-like because of pseudohyphae production; germ tube positive).
    • Candida tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei, C. glabrata (germ tube negative; non-albicans Candida).
    • Geotrichum candidum — forms true septate hyphae with arthroconidia.

3. Moulds / Filamentous Fungi (1½ marks)

  • Morphology — multicellular; grow as branching hyphae (tubular cells 2–10 µm wide). Mass of hyphae = mycelium. Two types of hyphae:
    • Septate hyphae — cross-walls (septa) divide hyphae into cells; e.g., Aspergillus, Dermatophytes.
    • Coenocytic (aseptate) hyphae — no cross-walls; multinucleate cytoplasm; e.g., Mucor, Rhizopus (Zygomycetes/Mucorales).
  • Reproduction — asexual by spores (conidia) borne on specialised structures (conidiophores); sexual by zygospores/ascospores.
  • Colony on SDA — cottony, woolly, powdery, velvety; various pigments (green-black Aspergillus, white-cream Trichophyton, grey-black Rhizopus).
  • Classification by spore-bearing structure
    • Conidia — asexual spores; macroconidia (large, multicellular) & microconidia (small, unicellular).
    • Sporangiospores — within a sac (sporangium); characteristic of Zygomycetes.

4. Dimorphic Fungi (1 mark)

  • Morphology — exist as mould (filamentous) at 25 °C (saprophytic form in environment) & yeast (or spherule) at 37 °C (parasitic form in host). This temperature-dependent dimorphism is a virulence factor.
  • Clinical relevance — must be cultured at both temperatures to confirm; BSL-3 containment required for culture (inhalation of conidia is hazardous).

Pneumocystis jirovecii (special mention)

Originally classified as protozoan (Pneumocystis carinii); now recognised as a fungus based on rRNA & ergosterol synthesis. Cysts seen on silver stain (GMS) in bronchoalveolar lavage — "crushed ping-pong balls" / "cup-shaped". Causes PCP pneumonia in HIV (CD4 <200). Does not grow on Sabouraud dextrose agar.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important bedside clue to fungal morphology is the KOH mount with calcofluor white: yeasts appear as oval budding cells; pseudohyphae have constrictions at septa (like sausages); true hyphae have parallel walls & true septa; aseptate (Mucorales) hyphae are broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, branching at 90° (right angles). This distinction is critical — Mucorales (mucormycosis) require urgent liposomal amphotericin B + surgical debridement (poor response to voriconazole, the first-line for Aspergillus). The COVID-19 pandemic saw a surge of COVID-associated mucormycosis (CAM) in India — uncontrolled diabetes, steroid therapy, and possibly iron overload from transfusions created the perfect storm. Remember: hyaline septate acute-angle branching = Aspergillus; broad aseptate right-angle branching = Mucorales — these two findings on histopathology can change antifungal choice within minutes.

Introduction

Biomedical waste (BMW) is any waste generated during diagnosis, treatment, or immunisation of humans or animals, in research, or in production/testing of biologicals. Approximately 10–25% of BMW is hazardous (infectious, toxic, or radioactive); improper management risks healthcare worker infections (HBV, HCV, HIV, TB), community exposure, and environmental pollution.

India regulates BMW under the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (amended 2018 & 2019) issued by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

Segregation — Colour Coding (4 marks)

Waste is segregated at source into colour-coded bags/containers as per Schedule I of BMW Rules 2016:

Colour code Type of waste Treatment & disposal
Yellow
  • Human anatomical waste — tissues, organs, body parts, foetus <20 weeks.
  • Animal anatomical waste.
  • Soiled waste — items contaminated with blood/body fluids (dressings, plaster casts, cotton swabs, blood bags).
  • Microbiological & biotechnology waste — cultures, stocks, vaccines (live), infectious material, discarded linen.
  • Expired/discarded medicines (cytotoxic drugs separate).
  • Incineration (anatomical, soiled, microbiological).
  • Plasma pyrolysis / deep burial (where incineration not available).
  • Autoclaving then shredding (microbiological).
Red
  • Contaminated recyclable plastic waste — IV tubes, catheters, urine bags, syringes (without needle), gloves.
  • Bottles, blood bags, microbiological plasticware.
  • Autoclaving / microwaving / chemical disinfection (1% sodium hypochlorite).
  • Shredding → recycling (only authorised recyclers).
White (Translucent, puncture-proof)
  • Sharps — needles, syringes with needles, scalpels, blades, broken glass, suture needles.
  • Autoclaving / dry heat sterilisation.
  • Needle cutters / destroyers → mutilation.
  • Final disposal in sharps pit or sent to metal recycler.
Blue (Translucent, puncture-proof)
  • Glassware — broken ampoules, vials, glass syringes, slides, coverslips.
  • Metallic body implants (after expiry of retention period — return to patient).
  • Disinfection (1% hypochlorite).
  • Return to manufacturer / recycling.
Black (separate; non-BMW)
  • General waste — food waste, paper, packaging (not contaminated).
  • Biomedical Rules do not apply — falls under Municipal Solid Waste Rules.
  • Municipal corporation collection & landfill.

Treatment Methods (2 marks)

  1. Incineration — high-temperature (≥850 °C) controlled burning; reduces waste volume by 90% & weight by 75%. Used for anatomical, soiled, microbiological waste. Not suitable for plastics (releases dioxins), PVC, halogenated compounds, heavy metals.
  2. Autoclaving — saturated steam under pressure (121 °C, 15 psi, 30–60 min); used for microbiological waste, soiled waste, plastic. Validates with biological indicator (G. stearothermophilus spores).
  3. Microwaving — 2450 MHz frequency; moist heat generated within waste. Pre-shredding often combined.
  4. Hydroclaving — modified autoclave with rotating blades; shredding & sterilisation in one step.
  5. Chemical disinfection — 1% sodium hypochlorite (10,000 ppm chlorine) for 30 min; for liquid waste, plastic, sharps (followed by mutilation).
  6. Plasma pyrolysis — high-temperature plasma (3000 °C) gasifies organic waste; minimal emissions; modern alternative to incineration.
  7. Deep burial — for institutions in rural areas without access to common BMW treatment facility (CBMWTF). Pit 2 m deep, lined with clay/lime; covered with soil after each layer; site away from water source.
  8. Sharp pit — concrete-lined pit for sharps after mutilation.
  9. Encapsulation — filling containers with plastic/metal, then sealing with cement/lime.
  10. Irradiation — gamma or electron beam; for specialised waste.

BMW Management Steps

  1. Segregation at source — colour-coded bags.
  2. Collection & transport — dedicated trolleys; labelled bags; closed transport within facility.
  3. Storage — ≤48 hours at room temp; refrigerated if longer.
  4. Treatment — on-site or Common Biomedical Waste Treatment Facility (CBMWTF).
  5. Disposal — landfill (residual), recycle (plastic, metal).
  6. Documentation — manifest system; barcoding; annual report to State Pollution Control Board.

Clinical Pearl

The single biggest risk in BMW is needle-stick injury — responsible for transmission of HBV (30% risk), HCV (3%), and HIV (0.3%) to healthcare workers. The "Do Not Recap" rule and immediate disposal into a white puncture-proof container at the point of generation are non-negotiable. Always use needle destroyers/cutters. In case of needle-stick: wash wound with soap & water (do not squeeze or apply caustic), assess source (HBV, HCV, HIV status), and start PEP within 72 hours (TDF + 3TC + DTG for 28 days) if source HIV-positive or unknown. Post-exposure prophylaxis with HBIG + hepatitis B vaccine booster if non-immune. Documentation & reporting to infection control committee is mandatory. The BMW Rules 2016 mandate an annual BMW audit and training of all healthcare workers — non-compliance can attract penalties up to ₹1 lakh per violation.

Clinical Identification

The 30-year-old woman with recurrent bilateral joint pain — especially involving the small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists, symmetric — is most consistent with Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), especially if associated with morning stiffness >1 h, fatigue, and laboratory findings of elevated ESR/CRP, positive rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-CCP antibodies, and anaemia of chronic disease.

Introduction

RA is a chronic, symmetric, progressive, autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis affecting primarily the synovial joints, with female preponderance (3:1; peak 30–50 years). It affects ~0.5–1% of the population; HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles (DR4, DR1) confer susceptibility. Pathology: chronic synovitis with pannus formation → cartilage & bone destruction → joint deformity.

Etiopathogenesis (2 marks)

  1. Genetic susceptibility — HLA-DRB1*0401, *0404, *0101 (shared epitope — QKRAA motif in β-chain); PTPN22, STAT4, PADI4 polymorphisms.
  2. Environmental triggers — smoking (interacts with HLA-DRB1, risk ×20), silica, mineral oil, obesity, nulliparity, breastfeeding; microbial triggers suspected (Porphyromonas gingivalis expresses citrullinated proteins; EBV, parvovirus B19, mycoplasma).
  3. Citrullination — peptidylarginine deiminase (PADI) enzymes convert arginine to citrulline in synovial proteins (vimentin, fibrin, type II collagen, α-enolase) — generating neoantigens.
  4. Autoimmune response
    • CD4+ T cell (Th1/Th17) activation against citrullinated peptides presented on HLA-DRB1 shared epitope.
    • B cell activation → plasma cells producing rheumatoid factor (IgM anti-IgG Fc) & anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies.
    • Immune complex deposition in synovium → complement activation (C5a, C3a) → chemotaxis.
  5. Synovitis & pannus formation — synovial macrophages & fibroblasts activated; secrete TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, RANKL → recruit neutrophils & monocytes; synovial lining hyperplasia; angiogenesis; pannus (granulation tissue) invades cartilage & bone.
  6. Joint destruction — RANKL activates osteoclasts → bone erosions; MMPs (1, 3, 13) degrade proteoglycans & collagen → cartilage loss.

Clinical Features (1 mark)

  • Articular — symmetric polyarthritis of small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists, MTPs); sparing DIP; morning stiffness >1 h; soft tissue swelling, warmth; reduced grip strength; later deformities: ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb, hammer toe, claw toe, cock-up deformity; atlanto-axial subluxation (neurological symptoms).
  • Extra-articular — rheumatoid nodules (extensor surfaces — olecranon, pressure points), Sjögren syndrome, pulmonary (ILD, pleural effusion, rheumatoid nodules, Caplan syndrome), cardiac (pericarditis, premature atherosclerosis), ocular (scleritis, episcleritis, Sjögren), vasculitis, Felty syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), amyloidosis, anaemia of chronic disease, osteoporosis, B-symptoms.

Investigations (1 mark)

  • Hb — normocytic normochromic anaemia of chronic disease.
  • ESR, CRP — elevated; correlate with disease activity.
  • Rheumatoid Factor (RF) — IgM anti-Fc IgG; positive in 70–80% (sensitive but not specific; also positive in SLE, Sjögren, chronic hepatitis, TB, sarcoid, old age).
  • Anti-CCP (anti-citrullinated peptide antibody, ACPA) — sensitivity 70%, specificity >95%; appears earlier than RF; predicts erosive disease.
  • ANA — exclude SLE; may be low-positive in RA.
  • Synovial fluid — inflammatory (WBC 2,000–50,000/µL, predominantly neutrophils); low viscosity; low complement; rheumatoid factor may be present; mucin clot poor.
  • Radiology — X-ray hands/wrists: periarticular osteopenia, soft tissue swelling, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, juxta-articular osteoporosis; MRI/ultrasound detect early synovitis & erosions.
  • HBV/HCV serology — exclude hepatitis C-related polyarthritis.

Classification (ACR/EULAR 2010) (1 mark)

Score-based (≥6/10 = definite RA):

  • Joint involvement (0–5): 1 large = 0; 2–10 large = 1; 1–3 small = 2; 4–10 small = 3; >10 joints (≥1 small) = 5.
  • Serology (0–3): negative RF & ACPA = 0; low-positive = 2; high-positive = 3.
  • Acute-phase reactants (0–1): normal CRP & ESR = 0; abnormal = 1.
  • Duration (0–1): <6 weeks = 0; ≥6 weeks = 1.

Treatment (1 mark)

  1. NSAIDs — symptomatic (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, COX-2 selective — celecoxib).
  2. Glucocorticoids — low-dose prednisolone (5–10 mg/day) or methylprednisolone pulses; bridge until DMARD works.
  3. Conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs)
    • Methotrexate — anchor drug; 7.5–25 mg/week oral/SC; folic acid supplementation.
    • Sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide — combination if MTX inadequate.
  4. Biologic DMARDs (bDMARDs)
    • TNF inhibitors — Infliximab, Adalimumab, Etanercept, Golimumab, Certolizumab.
    • IL-6 receptor — Tocilizumab, Sarilumab.
    • B-cell depletion — Rituximab (anti-CD20).
    • T-cell co-stimulation — Abatacept (CTLA4-Ig).
  5. Targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) — JAK inhibitors: Tofacitinib, Baricitinib, Upadacitinib.
  6. Treat-to-target — aim for remission (DAS28 <2.6) or low disease activity.
  7. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, joint protection, surgery (synovectomy, arthroplasty) for advanced disease.

Clinical Pearl

Anti-CCP antibody is the single most specific test for RA — positive in early RA (even before clinical symptoms) and predicts erosive disease. RF is more sensitive but less specific; ~20% of RA patients are seronegative (initially). The 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria replaced the old 1987 criteria to enable earlier diagnosis (within 6 weeks of symptom onset) because joint damage begins in the first 2 years. Treat-to-target strategy with methotrexate as anchor DMARD has revolutionised outcomes — early aggressive therapy prevents erosions and deformities. The cornerstone for monitoring is the DAS28 (Disease Activity Score-28) — calculated from 28 tender & swollen joints, ESR/CRP, and patient global assessment; DAS28 <2.6 = remission. Always screen for HBV, HCV, latent TB, and HIV before starting biologics — they can reactivate hepatitis or TB. Pregnancy: methotrexate is teratogenic (abortifacient); switch to sulfasalazine/hydroxychloroquine; certolizumab is preferred biologic (minimal placental transfer — no FcRn binding).

Definition

Innate immunity (also called native, natural, or non-specific immunity) is the first line of defence against pathogens that an individual is born with. It acts immediately (within minutes to hours), does not require prior exposure, and is non-specific — it recognises general patterns shared by many pathogens rather than specific epitopes.

Components (3 marks)

A. External / First-Line Defences (Physical & Chemical Barriers)

  • Skin — intact stratified squamous epithelium; low pH (5–6, sebum); continuous desquamation; antimicrobial peptides (defensins, cathelicidin — LL-37).
  • Mucous membranes — mucus traps microbes; ciliary action (respiratory mucociliary escalator); mucosal secretions (lysozyme, lactoferrin, peroxidase, secretory IgA — though IgA is adaptive, basally produced).
  • Gastric acid (pH 1–2); vaginal acidity (Lactobacillus); bile; pancreatic enzymes.
  • Commensal flora — competitive exclusion, bacteriocins, short-chain fatty acids; gut flora produces vitamin K, biotin.
  • Tears, saliva, sweat — lysozyme (cleaves N-acetylmuramic acid of bacterial cell wall).
  • Urine flow — flushing; low pH; prostatic secretions (zinc).
  • Blood-brain barrier; placental barrier.

B. Internal Cellular Defences

  • Phagocytes
    • Neutrophils — first responders; acute infection; pus formation; NETs (neutrophil extracellular traps).
    • Monocytes / macrophages — tissue macrophages (Kupffer cells in liver; alveolar macrophages; microglia; mesangial cells in kidney; Langerhans in skin); antigen presentation; chronic infection.
    • Dendritic cells — bridge innate & adaptive immunity; antigen presentation to naïve T cells.
  • Natural Killer (NK) cells — kill virus-infected & tumour cells via perforin/granzyme; recognise missing-self (MHC-I downregulation) via inhibitory KIR; ADCC via FcγRIII (CD16).
  • Eosinophils — parasitic helminth defence; allergy.
  • Basophils & mast cells — Type I hypersensitivity; parasitic defence; release histamine, heparin, proteases.
  • Platelets — β-lysins; thrombocidins; clotting traps microbes.
  • Epithelial cells — produce antimicrobial peptides, interferons, chemokines.

C. Internal Molecular Defences

  • Complement system — alternative & lectin pathways (independent of antibody); MAC (membrane attack complex) lysis; opsonisation (C3b); chemotaxis (C5a); anaphylaxis (C3a, C5a).
  • Acute-phase proteins — CRP, serum amyloid A, mannose-binding lectin (MBL), C-reactive protein, haptoglobin, ferritin, fibrinogen — produced by liver under IL-6 stimulation; opsonise microbes, activate complement.
  • Collectins & ficolins — surfactant proteins A & D; MBL; bind microbial carbohydrate patterns.
  • Pentraxins — CRP, SAP; bind phosphorylcholine on bacteria.
  • Interferons (Type I — IFN-α, IFN-β) — antiviral; produced by virus-infected cells; induce antiviral state (PKR, 2'5'-OAS, Mx proteins) in neighbouring cells.
  • Antimicrobial peptides — defensins (α, β), cathelicidin (LL-37), histatins, dermcidin; disrupt microbial membranes.
  • Cytokines — IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ (also Type II); IL-12, IL-18; chemokines (IL-8, MCP-1, RANTES).
  • Toll-like receptors (TLRs) — pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs) on macrophages, dendritic cells, epithelial cells; recognise pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs):
    • TLR2 — peptidoglycan (Gram-positive); TLR1/6 co-receptors.
    • TLR3 — dsRNA (viruses).
    • TLR4 — LPS (Gram-negative); with CD14 & MD-2.
    • TLR5 — flagellin.
    • TLR7/8 — ssRNA (viruses).
    • TLR9 — unmethylated CpG DNA.
  • NOD-like receptors (NLRs) — intracellular; NLRP3 inflammasome → caspase-1 → IL-1β.
  • RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) — cytoplasmic viral RNA sensors.
  • C-type lectin receptors (CLRs) — dectin-1 (β-glucan of fungi); mannose receptor.

Properties (3 marks)

  1. Innate (inborn) — present from birth; genetically determined; not acquired through exposure.
  2. Non-specific — broad-spectrum activity against any pathogen; does not distinguish between specific strains or antigens.
  3. Immediate (no lag phase) — acts within minutes–hours; no clonal expansion required.
  4. No immunological memory — repeated exposure does not produce a heightened or accelerated response (this is the hallmark of adaptive immunity).
  5. Pattern-based recognition — uses germline-encoded PRRs (TLRs, NLRs, RLRs, CLRs) that recognise conserved PAMPs (LPS, peptidoglycan, flagellin, dsRNA, CpG DNA) shared by many pathogens but absent in host.
  6. Not antigen-specific — does not require antigen processing/presentation on MHC.
  7. Species-wide (conserved) — similar mechanisms across individuals & even species; not subject to MHC restriction.
  8. Acts as a bridge to adaptive immunity — dendritic cells & macrophages process antigen and present to T cells; cytokines (IL-12, IFN-α) polarise Th1/Th2/Th17; complement & antibody enhance phagocytosis; provides co-stimulation (B7-CD28) essential for T cell priming.
  9. Triggered by tissue damage (DAMPs) — Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (HMGB1, ATP, uric acid, heat shock proteins, mitochondrial DNA) released by necrotic cells activate the same PRRs, producing sterile inflammation.
  10. Resistance not altered by prior exposure — first & hundredth encounter evoke the same response magnitude.

Comparison: Innate vs Adaptive

Feature Innate Adaptive
OnsetMinutes–hoursDays–weeks
SpecificityNon-specific (PAMPs)Epitope-specific
MemoryNoYes
DiversityLimited (germline-encoded)Vast (VDJ recombination)
CellsPhagocytes, NK, mast cellsT, B lymphocytes
MoleculesComplement, CRP, IFN-α/βAntibodies, cytokines

Clinical Pearl

Innate immunity determines the severity of sepsis — TLR4 polymorphisms (Asp299Gly) impair LPS recognition and predispose to Gram-negative septic shock, while also reducing atherosclerosis risk (chronic low-grade endotoxin exposure). The NLRP3 inflammasome links innate immunity to common diseases — gain-of-function mutations cause periodic fever syndromes (cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes — CAPS, familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome), treated dramatically with the IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra. The same inflammasome drives gout (MSU crystals), type 2 diabetes (islet amyloid), atherosclerosis (cholesterol crystals), and Alzheimer disease (amyloid-β) — illustrating how innate immunity is at the root of many chronic inflammatory diseases. Trained innate immunity — a recently described concept — shows that innate cells (monocytes, NK cells) can develop a memory-like response after exposure to BCG or β-glucan, providing non-specific protection against heterologous infections — a paradigm shift beyond the classical innate/adaptive dichotomy.

Definition

Graft-versus-Host Disease (GvHD / Graft-versus-Host Reaction — GvHR) is a potentially fatal complication that occurs when immunocompetent T lymphocytes from the donor (graft) recognise and attack the host (recipient) tissues as foreign, in a recipient who is immunocompromised and cannot reject the graft.

Triad of Conditions (Billingham's Criteria) for GvHD (1 mark)

  1. Graft must contain immunocompetent T lymphocytes — e.g., bone marrow, stem cell transplant, solid organ containing lymphoid tissue (liver, small bowel), unirradiated blood transfusion.
  2. Donor and recipient must be histo-incompatible — i.e., the recipient expresses antigens (HLA or minor antigens) absent in the donor, which the donor T cells recognise as foreign.
  3. Recipient must be immunocompromised (immunoincompetent) — cannot mount a host-versus-graft reaction to reject the donor cells. Examples: post-bone marrow transplant conditioning (chemotherapy/radiation), severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), neonates, immunosuppressive therapy.

Types (1 mark)

  • Acute GvHD — occurs <100 days post-transplant; classic target organs: skin (rash), liver (cholestasis, hyperbilirubinaemia), GIT (diarrhoea).
  • Chronic GvHD — occurs >100 days post-transplant; resembles autoimmune disease (Sjögren, scleroderma, lichen planus); affects skin, oral mucosa, liver, eyes, lungs (bronchiolitis obliterans), GIT, musculoskeletal; autoantibody formation.
  • Hyperacute GvHD — rare; within 1–2 weeks.

Pathogenesis (2 marks)

  1. Donor T cell recognition of host antigens
    • HLA mismatches (major) — even with HLA-identical sibling transplant, donor T cells recognise minor histocompatibility antigens (mHags — e.g., HA-1, HA-2, HY) presented on host APCs.
    • Host antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells) — survive conditioning; present host peptide-MHC to donor T cells.
  2. Donor T cell activation & expansion
    • CD4+ & CD8+ T cells activated via TCR + co-stimulation (CD28-B7).
    • Th1 polarisation — IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-α.
    • Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells kill host cells via perforin/granzyme & FasL.
  3. Cytokine storm — conditioning-induced tissue damage releases DAMPs (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) that amplify inflammation; synergistic with T cell cytokines.
  4. Tissue injury
    • Skin — basal cell apoptosis (Satterthwaite rash); bullous & desquamative in severe (TEN-like).
    • Liver — bile duct epithelial damage → cholestasis; hyperbilirubinaemia.
    • GIT — crypt cell apoptosis → watery/bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain.
    • Chronic — fibrosis, sclerosis, bronchiolitis obliterans.

Clinical Grading (acute GvHD) (1 mark)

Based on involvement of skin, liver, GIT (Glucksberg scale):

  • Grade I — rash <25% body surface; no liver/GI involvement.
  • Grade II — rash 25–50%; bilirubin 2–3 mg/dL; diarrhoea 500–1000 mL/day.
  • Grade III — generalized erythroderma; bilirubin 3–15 mg/dL; diarrhoea >1000 mL/day.
  • Grade IV — bullous rash/desquamation; bilirubin >15 mg/dL; severe diarrhoea/ileus; high mortality.

Prevention (1 mark)

  1. HLA matching — best to use HLA-identical sibling donor; if not, matched unrelated donor (MUD) from registries; haploidentical (half-matched) donors with post-transplant cyclophosphamide.
  2. T-cell depletion of graft — ex vivo removal of donor T cells (CD34+ positive selection or CD3/TCRαβ negative depletion); reduces GvHD but increases graft failure, EBV-LPD, and loss of graft-versus-leukaemia (GvL) effect.
  3. Prophylactic immunosuppression
    • Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) + methotrexate.
    • Cyclosporine + mycophenolate mofetil (non-myeloablative transplants).
    • Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) — for haploidentical transplants; eliminates alloreactive T cells.
    • Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) — T-cell depletion in vivo.
  4. Irrradiation of blood products (25 Gy) — prevents transfusion-associated GvHD (TA-GvHD) in immunocompromised recipients; leukodepletion alone is insufficient.

Treatment of Established GvHD

  • Grade I — topical steroids (skin), no systemic.
  • Grade II–IV — high-dose methylprednisolone (1–2 mg/kg/day); if steroid-refractory: ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor — FDA-approved 2019); extracorporeal photopheresis; anti-TNF (infliximab); IL-2 receptor antibody (basiliximab); mesenchymal stem cells; ABLE 2/3 monoclonal antibodies.
  • Chronic GvHD — calcineurin inhibitors + steroids; ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor — FDA-approved for chronic GvHD); belumosudil (ROCK2 inhibitor — 2021); ruxolitinib (2021).

Clinical Pearl

TA-GvHD (transfusion-associated GvHD) — occurs when unirradiated cellular blood components (RBCs, platelets, non-leukodepleted whole blood) are transfused to an immunocompromised recipient (chemotherapy, BMT, congenital immunodeficiency, neonatal exchange transfusion, intrauterine transfusion); donor T cells engraft & attack host. Mortality is >90% — no effective treatment. Prevention: irradiate all cellular blood products (25 Gy) given to immunocompromised patients. Even immunocompetent recipients can develop TA-GvHD if donor is homozygous for one of the recipient's HLA haplotypes (directed donation from first-degree relatives) — hence irradiation is mandatory for all directed donations from relatives. In stem cell transplant, a delicate balance exists between GvHD (harmful) and graft-versus-leukaemia (GvL) effect (beneficial — donor T cells kill residual leukaemia cells); excessive T-cell depletion reduces GvHD but increases relapse. This is why mild chronic GvHD is sometimes left untreated — it correlates with lower leukaemia relapse.

Definition

Chemical sterilants are liquid or gaseous chemicals capable of destroying all microbial life — including bacteria (vegetative & spores), viruses, fungi, and protozoa — achieving sterility (SAL 10⁻⁶). They are used when heat (autoclave, dry heat) is unsuitable — i.e., for heat- or moisture-sensitive items such as endoscopes, electrical equipment, plastics, and optical instruments.

Distinction

  • High-level disinfectants (HLDs) — kill all microbes except high numbers of bacterial spores; can become sterilants with extended exposure (>3–10 h depending on agent). E.g., glutaraldehyde, OPA, H₂O₂, peracetic acid.
  • Intermediate / low-level disinfectants — alcohols, phenolics, QACs, halogens; not sporicidal.

Ideal Properties of a Chemical Sterilant

  • Wide antimicrobial spectrum (including spores, mycobacteria, viruses, fungi).
  • Rapid action; long reuse life.
  • Compatibility with materials (no corrosion, no swelling, no discolouration of rubber/plastic/metal).
  • Low toxicity to staff & patients (non-irritant, non-sensitising, non-carcinogenic).
  • Easy to monitor concentration with test strips.
  • Reasonable cost; easily disposable; minimal environmental hazard.
  • Not inactivated by organic matter.

Commonly Used Chemical Sterilants / HLDs (4 marks)

Agent Concentration Activity Uses & Limitations
Glutaraldehyde 2% aqueous (Cidex) HLD 20–45 min @ 25 °C; sterilant 10 h Endoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment, anaesthesia equipment, dialysers, rubber & plastic items. Activated by alkalising to pH 7.5–8.5; reuse for 14–28 days (check MRC test strip ≥1.5%). Limitations: irritant vapour (use closed container, ventilation, PPE); fixing protein (must pre-clean items); not sporicidal at short exposure; pulmonary sensitisation; M. chelonei outbreak risk if reused too long.
Ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA) 0.55% HLD 12 min @ 20 °C; sterilant 6 h Replacement for glutaraldehyde — no activation, less irritating vapour, faster action. Stains skin/proteins grey; repeated exposure can sensitise urology staff. Higher cost.
Hydrogen peroxide 7.5% solution; 6 mg/L vapour-phase (Sterrad) HLD 30 min; sterilant 3–6 h (solution); vapour plasma 45–75 min Heat-sensitive instruments, endoscopes, electrical equipment. No toxic residue (decomposes to water & oxygen). Limitations: incompatible with paper, cellulose, copper, brass; penetrates lumens poorly unless plasma.
Peracetic acid 0.2–0.35% Sterilant 12–30 min @ 50–55 °C Steris System 1 — liquid chemical sterilant for immersible instruments (rigid endoscopes, surgical instruments); single-use; no reuse; rapid. Limitations: corrodes some metals; inactivated by organic matter; must be used in closed machine; items must be used immediately (no storage).
Ethylene oxide (EtO) gas 450–1200 mg/L at 37–63 °C, 40–60% RH Sterilant 2–6 h; aeration 8–12 h Heat- & moisture-sensitive items: endoscopes, electrical equipment, plastics, catheters, sutures, implantable devices. Limitations: carcinogen, flammable (use 12/88 with Freon or 100% EtO); long cycle; requires aeration; Alkylates DNA/RNA/proteins; trapped gas can harm patient. Biological indicator: Bacillus atrophaeus.
Formaldehyde vapour (LTSF) Low-temperature steam formaldehyde — 2% at 70–80 °C Sterilant 3–6 h Heat-sensitive items; alternative to EtO. Carcinogen; requires ventilation & aeration. Less common now.
H₂O₂ plasma (Sterrad) 6 mg/L H₂O₂ vapour + radiofrequency plasma Sterilant 45–75 min @ <50 °C Heat-sensitive medical devices, endoscopes, electrical instruments. No toxic residue; safe for staff. Limitations: small chamber; cannot process liquids, paper, cellulose, linen; lumen <1 mm diameter problematic.
Ozone 5–14 mg/L Sterilant 4–6 h @ 30–35 °C Heat-sensitive items; uses oxygen & electricity — no toxic residue. Limited penetration.
Peracetic acid + H₂O₂ (System 33) Combination HLD 30 min Endoscope disinfection; one-shot system; single-use solution. Strong odour; irritating.
Hypochlorite 1:10 dilution = 5000 ppm; 1:50 = 1000 ppm HLD; sporicidal (slow) Blood spills, surfaces, dialysis equipment. Limitations: corrosive, inactivated by organic matter, no residual activity; irritating; damages metals/rubber.

Applications in Healthcare (1 mark)

  1. Endoscopes (flexible & rigid) — glutaraldehyde, OPA, peracetic acid. Critical: duodenoscopes (ERCP) carry high infection risk — prefer ethylene oxide or peracetic acid for high-level disinfection due to elevator channel complexity.
  2. Respiratory therapy equipment — glutaraldehyde; auto-disinfector machines.
  3. Anaesthesia equipment — masks, breathing circuits, laryngoscope blades; glutaraldehyde/OPA.
  4. Haemodialysis equipment — 4% formaldehyde, peracetic acid, hypochlorite.
  5. Surgical instruments with optics — cameras, light cables; peracetic acid or H₂O₂ plasma.
  6. Dental instruments — glutaraldehyde (handpieces), OPA.
  7. Electrical/electronic equipment — EtO, H₂O₂ plasma.
  8. Implantable devices (single-use) — gamma radiation at manufacturer; EtO for items incompatible with radiation.
  9. Surface & spill disinfection — hypochlorite, alcohol, QACs, phenolics.
  10. Plastic disposable items — EtO, gamma radiation (at manufacturer).

Sterilization Monitoring

  • MRC (minimum recommended concentration) test strips — for glutaraldehyde (≥1.5%), OPA, peracetic acid; check before each use.
  • Biological indicators — Bacillus atrophaeus spores for EtO & dry heat; G. stearothermophilus for H₂O₂ plasma, peracetic acid.
  • Chemical indicators — Class 4–6 strips inside each pack.

Clinical Pearl

The single biggest lesson in chemical sterilisation is the outbreak of atypical mycobacteria (M. abscessus, M. chelonae) in post-laparoscopy and post-endoscopy patients — these organisms survive standard glutaraldehyde exposure (especially reused solution past expiry) by forming biofilm in instrument channels. Prevention: (1) meticulous manual cleaning with enzymatic detergent before disinfection; (2) discard glutaraldehyde after 14 days (or per MRC strip); (3) use automated endoscope reprocessors (AER) with filtered water & 70% alcohol flush to dry channels; (4) store endoscopes vertically in a drying cabinet; culture regularly. For duodenoscopes (ERCP), the FDA in 2015 issued a safety alert after multiple MDR-organism outbreaks — now recommends EtO sterilisation or liquid chemical sterilant (peracetic acid) after HLD. The take-home: HLD reduces microbial load but does not sterilise; for instruments entering sterile tissue (critical items), only true sterilisation is acceptable.

Definition

Cytokine storm (also called cytokine release syndrome — CRS, hypercytokinaemia) is a systemic, uncontrolled, excessive inflammatory response characterised by a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines — predominantly IL-6, IL-1, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-8, IL-10, IL-18 — leading to multi-organ dysfunction, capillary leak, shock, and potentially death. The term was coined by Ferrara et al. (1993) in the context of graft-versus-host disease.

Pathogenesis (2 marks)

  1. Trigger
    • Infections — SARS-CoV-2 (severe COVID-19), influenza H1N1, SARS, MERS, EBV, CMV, dengue, Ebola, Staphylococcal enterotoxin B, Streptococcal toxic shock.
    • Immunotherapy — CAR-T cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel), bispecific T-cell engagers (blinatumomab), therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (rituximab, alemtuzumab), checkpoint inhibitors (ipilimumab, nivolumab), OKT3 (muromonab).
    • Autoinflammatory / autoimmune — macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), secondary HLH (haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis), adult-onset Still's disease, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
    • Graft-versus-host disease (post-HSCT).
    • Drugs — amphotericin B, rituximab (first dose), some chemotherapeutics.
  2. Immune cell activation
    • Antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells) activated via PRRs (TLRs, NLRs) → release IL-6, IL-1, TNF-α.
    • T cells activated → IFN-γ, GM-CSF; recruits & activates more macrophages (positive feedback loop).
    • NK cells, NKT cells, mast cells, endothelial cells all participate.
    • NLRP3 inflammasome activates caspase-1 → IL-1β & IL-18 (pyroptosis).
  3. Self-amplifying loop — cytokines activate more immune cells → more cytokine release → uncontrolled cascade.
  4. Endothelial activation & dysfunction
    • Angiopoietin-2 release, vascular leakage, complement activation, contact system (bradykinin), coagulation cascade.
    • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — microthrombi, bleeding.
  5. End-organ damage
    • Lungs — ARDS, diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membranes.
    • Heart — myocardial dysfunction, troponin rise, arrhythmias.
    • Kidneys — acute tubular necrosis, AKI.
    • Liver — transaminitis, hyperbilirubinaemia.
    • CNS — encephalopathy, seizures, raised ICP (CAR-T-related encephalopathy syndrome — CRES).
    • Coagulation — DIC, thrombosis, bleeding.

Key Cytokines & Their Roles

  • IL-6 — central mediator; hepatic acute-phase response; B-cell differentiation; T-cell activation; correlates with severity & mortality.
  • IL-1β — pyrogen; inflammasome-driven; osteoclast activation.
  • TNF-α — pro-inflammatory; cachexia; endothelial activation; septicaemia.
  • IFN-γ — macrophage activation; key for haemophagocytic syndrome.
  • IL-8 — neutrophil chemotaxis.
  • IL-10 — anti-inflammatory counter-regulatory (often paradoxically elevated).
  • IL-18 — inflammasome; synergistic with IL-12 to induce IFN-γ.

Clinical Features

  • Systemic — high fever (often >39 °C), rigors, fatigue, myalgia, headache.
  • Hypotension & shock — distributive (capillary leak); vasopressor requirement.
  • Respiratory — tachypnoea, hypoxia, ARDS.
  • Cardiac — tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, troponin elevation.
  • Renal — oliguria, AKI.
  • Hepatic — jaundice, transaminitis.
  • Neurological — confusion, headache, seizures, CRES (immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome — ICANS).
  • Haematological — cytopenias (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia), DIC, ferritin >10,000.

Diagnosis

  • CRP (markedly elevated), procalcitonin, ferritin (often >10,000 ng/mL), D-dimer, LDH (markedly raised), triglycerides (elevated), fibrinogen (low — consumption), liver function tests, troponin, CK.
  • Cytokine panels — IL-6 (most useful; >80 pg/mL severe), IL-10, IFN-γ, sIL-2Rα (sCD25) elevated.
  • HLH criteria (HScore) — fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias (≥2 lineages), hypertriglyceridaemia (>265 mg/dL) or hypofibrinogenaemia (<150 mg/dL), haemophagocytosis on bone marrow, low NK cell activity, ferritin >500 ng/mL, sCD25 >2400 U/mL.
  • Imaging — chest CT (ground-glass opacities, ARDS), abdominal ultrasound (hepatosplenomegaly), echo (cardiac dysfunction).

Management (2 marks)

  1. Identify & treat trigger — anti-microbials, antivirals; stop offending drug.
  2. Supportive care — ICU admission, vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, ECMO in refractory ARDS.
  3. Anti-cytokine therapy
    • Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) — FDA-approved for CRS (CAR-T); also for severe COVID-19.
    • Siltuximab — anti-IL-6 monoclonal; COVID-19.
    • Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) — for MAS/HLH, COVID-19 with hyperinflammation.
    • Corticosteroids — dexamethasone (RECOVERY trial — COVID-19), methylprednisolone.
    • Lenzilumab — anti-GM-CSF (CAR-T & COVID).
    • Emapalumab — anti-IFN-γ (FDA-approved for primary HLH).
    • Ruxolitinib — JAK1/2 inhibitor.
    • Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).
    • Plasma exchange / CRRT — cytokine removal.
  4. Specific for CAR-T CRS
    • Grade 1 — supportive.
    • Grade ≥2 — tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg); may repeat after 8 h.
    • Grade ≥3 — add dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h.
  5. HLH-94 protocol — etoposide + dexamethasone + cyclosporine for primary HLH; intrathecal methotrexate for CNS disease.

Clinical Pearl

Cytokine storm became globally familiar during the COVID-19 pandemic — severe COVID-19 is driven not by direct viral damage alone but by a hyperinflammatory host response. The RECOVERY trial (2020) showed dexamethasone 6 mg/day reduced 28-day mortality by 35% in ventilated COVID patients — first drug to show survival benefit. Tocilizumab (RECOVERY 2021) further reduced mortality when added for hypoxic patients with elevated CRP. Anti-IL-6 (tocilizumab) and anti-IL-1 (anakinra) have transformed CAR-T therapy — they made previously fatal CRS manageable, enabling widespread adoption of CAR-T for leukaemia/lymphoma. The ASTCT consensus grading (2019) for CRS uses fever + hypotension + hypoxia criteria (not the older Penn scale) — grade 1 = fever only; grade 2 = hypotension responding to fluids or hypoxia responding to O₂; grade 3 = hypotension on vasopressors or hypoxia on high-flow O₂; grade 4 = multiple vasopressors or positive pressure ventilation. For ICANS (neurotoxicity), the ICE score (10-point orientation) is used. Ferritin >10,000 ng/mL is a strong pointer to MAS/HLH — consider anakinra early.

Definition

Mutation is a stable, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of the genome of an organism. It can occur spontaneously (due to errors in DNA replication, tautomeric shifts, deamination, depurination) or be induced by mutagens (physical — UV, X-ray, gamma-ray; chemical — nitrous acid, alkylating agents, base analogues; biological — transposons, viral integration).

Rate: ~10⁻⁶ to 10⁻¹⁰ per gene per generation in bacteria (E. coli ~10⁻⁷ per gene per generation).

Classification

A. By Mechanism / Molecular Nature (3 marks)

1. Point Mutation

Change in a single nucleotide. Sub-types:

  • Substitution
    • Transition — purine → purine (A ↔ G) or pyrimidine → pyrimidine (C ↔ T). Most common (≈70%).
    • Transversion — purine → pyrimidine or vice versa (A ↔ C, A ↔ T, G ↔ C, G ↔ T). Less common.
  • By functional consequence:
    • Silent (synonymous) — codon changes but encodes same amino acid (due to codon degeneracy); no phenotypic change.
    • Missense — codon changes to encode a different amino acid. Conservative (similar aa — mild effect) or non-conservative (dissimilar aa — severe, e.g., HbS — Glu→Val at position 6 of β-globin).
    • Nonsense — codon changes to a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) → premature termination → truncated, usually non-functional protein (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
    • Stop-loss — stop codon → sense codon → elongated protein.
2. Frameshift Mutation

Insertion or deletion of nucleotides in a number not divisible by 3 → shifts the reading frame → entirely different amino acid sequence downstream → usually premature stop codon → non-functional protein. E.g., Tay-Sachs (HEXA), Hb Wayne.

3. Insertions / Deletions (InDels)
  • Small (1–1000 bp) — frameshift if not multiple of 3.
  • Large — deletion of entire gene or exon; e.g., α-thalassaemia (--SEA deletion), Duchenne (deletion of dystrophin exons).
4. Dynamic / Expansion Mutation (Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion)

Expansion of unstable trinucleotide repeat sequences beyond a threshold during meiosis — causes anticipation (worse phenotype in successive generations). Examples:

  • Huntington disease — CAG in HTT (≥36 repeats).
  • Fragile X — CGG in FMR1 (>200 repeats; full mutation).
  • Myotonic dystrophy — CTG in DMPK (>50 repeats).
  • Friedreich ataxia — GAA in FXN (>66 repeats).
  • Spinocerebellar ataxias — CAG in various genes.
5. Copy Number Variation (CNV)

Duplication or deletion of large segments (>1 kb) — e.g., Hb Lepore (δβ fusion), dup 22q11.2 (cat eye); CMT1A (PMP22 duplication).

6. Chromosomal Mutations
  • Numerical
    • Aneuploidy — trisomy 21 (Down), 18 (Edward), 13 (Patau), X (Klinefelter XXY), monosomy X (Turner).
    • Polyploidy — triploidy, tetraploidy (lethal in humans; common in plants).
  • Structural
    • Deletion (5p- Cri-du-chat, 11p- aniridia/WAGR, 22q11.2 DiGeorge).
    • Duplication (Pallister-Killian 12p isochromosome).
    • Inversion (Factor VIII gene intron 22 inversion in Haemophilia A).
    • Translocation
      • Reciprocal — Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11) — CML (BCR-ABL fusion).
      • Robertsonian — centromeric fusion of acrocentric chromosomes; t(14;21) — Down syndrome (translocation type).
    • Ring chromosome, isochromosome.
7. Conditional / Reversible
  • Suppressor mutation — second mutation that restores original phenotype (intragenic or intergenic).
  • Back mutation — reversion to wild-type.

B. By Effect on Phenotype (1 mark)

  • Loss-of-function — reduced or abolished protein activity; usually recessive (e.g., PKU, albinism).
  • Gain-of-function — new/ enhanced activity; usually dominant (e.g., Huntington disease, achondroplasia FGFR3, RET in MEN2).
  • Dominant-negative — mutant protein interferes with wild-type (e.g., p53, Marfan — mutant fibrillin disrupts normal fibrillin assembly).
  • Conditional / temperature-sensitive — phenotype only under certain conditions (e.g., Siamese cat coat colour — tyrosinase active only below body temperature).
  • Lethal — causes death (often embryonic).
  • Neutral / Silent — no phenotypic effect.

C. By Origin / Cell Type (1 mark)

  • Germ-line — in gametes; heritable; affects every cell of offspring (e.g., BRCA1 mutation in breast cancer family).
  • Somatic — in body cells; not heritable; causes cancer & mosaicism (e.g., TP53 mutation in lung cancer).

In Bacteria — Special Types

  • Auxotrophic mutant — loses ability to synthesise an essential nutrient; requires supplementation (e.g., his⁻ mutant of Salmonella in Ames test).
  • Antibiotic-resistant mutant — e.g., rifampicin-resistant rpoB mutant; MRSA (mecA).
  • Conditionally lethal / temperature-sensitive (ts) — grows at permissive temperature (30 °C), dies at restrictive (42 °C); useful for vaccine strains.
  • Phase variation — reversible on/off switching of gene expression (e.g., flagellin in Salmonella).
  • Antigenic variation — changes surface antigen (e.g., Neisseria pili, Borrelia VlsE, trypanosomes).

Causes / Mutagens

  • Base analogues — 5-bromouracil (mimics thymine); 2-aminopurine (mimics adenine).
  • Alkylating agents — EMS, MNNG, nitrogen mustard; add alkyl groups to bases → mispairing.
  • Deaminating agents — nitrous acid (HNO₂); converts adenine → hypoxanthine (pairs with C), cytosine → uracil.
  • Intercalating agents — acridine orange, proflavin, ethidium bromide; insert between base pairs → frameshift.
  • Hydroxylamine — modifies cytosine → pairs with adenine.
  • UV radiation — thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer).
  • Ionising radiation — X-ray, gamma-ray; single- & double-strand breaks.
  • Replication errors — slippage (microsatellite instability); tautomeric shifts.
  • Transposons / Insertion sequences — move within genome; disrupt genes.
  • Viral integration — HPV E6/E7 inactivate p53/Rb.

  • Direct repair — photolyase (in bacteria; not humans); O⁶-methylguanine methyltransferase (MGMT).
  • Base excision repair (BER) — DNA glycosylase; for deaminated/oxidised bases.
  • Nucleotide excision repair (NER) — for bulky lesions (thymine dimers); defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Mismatch repair (MMR) — recognises mispaired bases; defective in hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome).
  • Double-strand break repair — homologous recombination (BRCA1/2 — hereditary breast/ovarian cancer) & non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).

The Ames test uses his⁻ Salmonella typhimurium to detect mutagens — if a chemical induces reverse mutation to his⁺, the bacteria grow on histidine-free medium → mutagen identified. Adding rat liver S9 fraction mimics mammalian metabolism — detects procarcinogens (e.g., aflatoxin B1, benzopyrene) that are activated in vivo. ~85% of known human carcinogens are mutagens in the Ames test — making it a powerful screening tool. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumours is now standard of care — exemplified by FoundationOne CDx covering 324 genes. Hotspot mutations (e.g., KRAS codon 12, TP53 codon 248, BRAF V600) recur across cancer types because they occur in critical functional domains.

Definition

Healthcare-associated infection (HAI) — also called nosocomial infection or hospital-acquired infection — is an infection occurring in a patient that was not present or incubating at the time of admission. The CDC/NHSN defines HAI by the following criteria:

  1. Infection develops ≥48 hours after admission to a healthcare facility.
  2. Infection develops within 30 days after discharge from a hospital (or 90 days if an implant was placed).
  3. Infection develops within 30 days (or 90 days with implant) of a surgical procedure.
  4. Infection develops in a patient receiving outpatient or home-care services (wound care, dialysis, IV therapy, catheterisation).
  5. Infection in a healthcare worker acquired through occupational exposure.

Epidemiology

  • WHO estimates 7–10% of hospitalised patients in developed countries and 10–25% in developing countries acquire an HAI.
  • ICU patients have 5–10× higher risk.
  • In India, HAI rates range from 10–30% depending on facility & surveillance methodology.
  • Commonest HAIs: urinary tract infection (UTI — 30–40%), surgical site infection (SSI — 20–25%), pneumonia (VAP — 10–15%), bloodstream infection (CLABSI — 5–10%).

  • Patient — extremes of age, immunosuppression, malnutrition, diabetes, chronic illness, prolonged hospitalisation, severity of underlying disease.
  • Device-related — urinary catheter, central venous catheter, endotracheal tube, haemodialysis catheter, surgical drain.
  • Procedure-related — surgery, prolonged operative time, emergency procedure, contaminated wound class, improper antibiotic prophylaxis.
  • Environment — overcrowding, inadequate ventilation, contaminated water/air, poor sterilisation, contaminated disinfectants.
  • Antibiotic pressure — broad-spectrum antibiotic use selects multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRPA, CRAB).

  • Endogenous — patient's own flora (skin, gut, respiratory); ~50% of HAIs.
  • Exogenous — healthcare workers' hands (most common cross-transmission), contaminated equipment, environment (fomites, water, air), other patients.
  • Parenteral — contaminated IV fluids, blood products, injections.

  • Contact (most common) — direct (patient-to-patient, HCW-to-patient); indirect (via hands, equipment, environment).
  • Droplet — respiratory droplets >5 µm, <1 m distance (influenza, pertussis, RSV, mumps).
  • Airborne — droplet nuclei <5 µm, >1 m distance (TB, measles, varicella, aspergillosis).
  • Vehicle — contaminated food, water, medications, devices.
  • Vector — mosquitoes (malaria in hospital), flies.

Prevention — WHO Core Components

  1. Infection prevention & control (IPC) programme with dedicated team.
  2. National guidelines & facility SOPs.
  3. Surveillance — facility-based, with feedback.
  4. Antibiotic stewardship — restrict broad-spectrum use, de-escalate, monitor resistance.
  5. Hand hygiene — WHO 5 Moments; alcohol-based handrub.
  6. Personal protective equipment (PPE).
  7. Sterilisation & disinfection — Spaulding-based.
  8. Care bundles — VAP bundle (head-of-bed elevation, daily sedation interruption, oral chlorhexidine, subglottic secretion drainage, DVT prophylaxis); CLABSI bundle (full barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin prep, avoidance of femoral site, daily review of line necessity); CAUTI bundle (sterile insertion, closed drainage, daily review, no routine bladder irrigation).
  9. Isolation precautions — standard; contact; droplet; airborne.
  10. Environmental cleaning & waste management.
  11. HCW vaccination & occupational health.

Site-specific definitions, device-associated infection rates reported as per 1000 device-days. Hospital infection control committee (HICC) reviews monthly data, performs root-cause analysis of clusters, feeds back to clinicians.

Clinical Pearl

WHO's 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene — before patient contact; before aseptic task; after body fluid exposure risk; after patient contact; after contact with patient surroundings — is the single most cost-effective intervention. Alcohol-based handrub (60–80% ethanol or isopropyl) reduces HAI rates by 30–50% and is faster than soap-and-water (20 sec vs 60 sec). However, alcohol does NOT kill C. difficile spores — use soap & water for suspected/confirmed CDI. The rise of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE — NDM, KPC, OXA-48) in Indian ICUs is alarming — a single CRE-positive patient can contaminate the entire environment (bed rails, IV poles, sinks) within 24 h, requiring aggressive contact precautions, dedicated equipment, and terminal room cleaning with bleach + UV-C. The future is whole-genome sequencing for outbreak investigation — distinguishes true transmission events from coincidental unrelated strains within hours.

Introduction

Immunoglobulin M (IgM) is the largest antibody (≈900 kDa; 5 subunits) and the first immunoglobulin produced in the primary immune response. It is the third most abundant serum Ig (~5–10% of total Ig; 0.5–2 mg/mL). IgM is also the first immunoglobulin synthesised by the fetus (≈20 weeks gestation) and the first to appear in phylogeny (even in jawless fish — primitive IgM-like molecules).

Structure (1 mark)

  • Pentamer in serum — 5 IgM monomers (each 180 kDa) joined by a J-chain (joining chain, 15 kDa) via disulfide bonds. Total molecular weight ~900 kDa.
  • Monomer on B cell surface — expressed as membrane-bound monomer (mIgM) — functions as B-cell receptor (BCR) on naïve B cells.
  • Heavy chain (μ) — 5 domains (Vμ + 4 Cμ); lacks hinge region.
  • Light chain — κ or λ.
  • 10 antigen-binding sites (pentamer) — high avidity (functional affinity) despite lower intrinsic affinity per Fab than IgG.
  • Half-life — ~5 days (short; in serum ~5 days; on B cell surface longer).
  • Does NOT cross placenta — too large. Fetal IgM is self-produced; elevated fetal/neonatal IgM indicates congenital infection (TORCH).

Functions (4 marks)

  1. Primary immune response antibody
    • First Ig produced after antigen exposure (within 5–7 days; peaks 1–2 weeks).
    • Naïve B cells express surface IgM (BCR); on antigen binding, proliferate and secrete IgM before class-switching to IgG/IgA.
    • IgM is later replaced by IgG (class-switched) — but memory B cells retain IgM expression.
  2. Most potent complement activator (classical pathway)
    • Single pentameric IgM bound to antigen can activate complement — binds C1q via Fc.
    • IgM is ~400–1000× more efficient than IgG in activating complement (IgG requires ≥2 molecules spaced 30–40 nm apart).
    • C1q binds to Fc portion of μ chain → C1r–C1s → C4, C2 → C3 convertase → C3b → opsonisation & MAC lysis.
    • Important for bacteriolysis (Gram-negative), virus neutralisation.
  3. Agglutination
    • 10 antigen-binding sites (pentamer) → efficient cross-linking of particulate antigens (bacteria, RBCs).
    • IgM is ~100× more effective than IgG at agglutination.
    • Basis for blood typing (ABO) — anti-A and anti-B are IgM; cause immediate RBC agglutination → transfusion reactions.
    • Widal test (Salmonella O antigen), Weil-Felix (Rickettsia), VDRL (Treponema) — IgM-based agglutination tests.
  4. First line of defence — intravascular neutralisation
    • Largely confined to intravascular space (80%); limited extravascular penetration due to large size.
    • Important in bacteraemia & viraemia — rapidly activates complement & clears microbes.
  5. Opsonisation
    • Direct — via complement C3b (more important than IgG Fc for IgM).
    • Indirect — complement receptor on phagocytes (CR1, CR3) recognises C3b on IgM-coated microbe.
  6. Cytolysis (MAC — Membrane Attack Complex)
    • Complement activation → C5b-C9 → MAC → osmotic lysis of Gram-negative bacteria, enveloped viruses.
  7. Antigen receptor on naïve B cells (mIgM-BCR)
    • Naïve B cells co-express IgM & IgD on surface; BCR complex (Igα/Igβ) transduces signal → B-cell activation, proliferation, class-switching, memory.
    • Loss of surface IgM → B cell cannot respond to antigen.
  8. Natural antibodies
    • Polyreactive low-affinity IgM produced by B-1 cells (CD5+); without prior antigen exposure.
    • Recognise common microbial patterns (phosphorylcholine, LPS) & self antigens (e.g., ABO isohemagglutinins — anti-A, anti-B in individuals lacking that antigen).
    • First-line innate-like defence against blood-borne pathogens.
  9. Diagnostic marker of recent / acute infection
    • IgM appears first, peaks 1–2 weeks, declines by 6–8 weeks; replaced by IgG.
    • Detection of specific IgM indicates current or recent infection — TORCH (toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV, HIV, hepatitis A/E, dengue, leptospirosis, syphilis VDRL, EBV VCA, mycoplasma).
    • In neonate — elevated IgM indicates congenital infection (maternal IgG crosses placenta, IgM does not).
  10. Rheumatoid factor (RF)
    • IgM antibody against Fc portion of IgG — diagnostic marker of rheumatoid arthritis (~70–80% sensitive).
    • Forms immune complexes → complement activation → joint damage.
  11. Cryoglobulins & cold agglutinins
    • IgM with anti-I specificity — cold agglutinin disease (mycoplasma pneumonia, EBV infection); haemolysis at low temperature.
    • Type II cryoglobulinaemia — monoclonal IgM with anti-IgG activity (HCV-associated).
  12. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia
    • IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; hyperviscosity syndrome (headache, visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding); treated with rituximab + chemotherapy.

Clinical Significance

  • Selective IgM deficiency — rare; recurrent sinopulmonary & GI infections, sepsis, autoimmune disease.
  • Hyper-IgM syndrome — CD40L deficiency (X-linked); failure of class switching → high IgM, low IgG/IgA/IgE; recurrent pyogenic & opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium).
  • Neonatal screening — elevated IgM in cord blood or neonatal serum suggests congenital infection (TORCH).

Clinical Pearl

The single most useful diagnostic role of IgM is in acute infection diagnosis: detection of specific IgM antibodies in serum is a strong indicator of current or recent infection because IgM is the first antibody produced, peaks at 1–2 weeks, and disappears by 6–8 weeks (while IgG persists for years). For example, HEV IgM in a pregnant woman with acute hepatitis → recent hepatitis E (high mortality in pregnancy); rubella IgM in early pregnancy → risk of congenital rubella syndrome (consider termination); dengue IgM (NS1 + IgM) in febrile patient → dengue. However, IgM can persist for months in some infections (CMV, EBV, parvovirus B19) or even reappear on reactivation — so a positive IgM alone does not always mean acute infection. Cross-reactivity is also a problem — dengue IgM cross-reacts with other flaviviruses (Zika, JE, yellow fever vaccine). The pentameric structure of IgM (10 binding sites) explains why it is the most efficient complement activator — a single IgM molecule can trigger the classical pathway, whereas ≥2 IgG molecules are required. This is why IgM is the first responder in the immune response — it achieves what IgG achieves in quantity through quality.

Definition

A superantigen (SAg) is a class of microbial protein exotoxin that, unlike conventional antigens, bypasses normal antigen processing & presentation and potently activates a large fraction (5–30%) of the host's T cell population. This leads to massive pro-inflammatory cytokine release (cytokine storm), T-cell proliferation, and potentially toxic shock.

Mechanism of Action (3 marks)

  1. Conventional antigen
    • Antigen is taken up by antigen-presenting cell (APC); processed into short peptides (8–22 aa); peptide loaded onto MHC-II groove; presented to TCR.
    • Only T cells with the specific TCR Vβ complementary to that peptide-MHC are activated (frequency ~1 in 10⁵–10⁶ T cells).
  2. Superantigen mechanism
    • Binds outside the peptide-binding groove of MHC class II on APC (to the α-chain or β-chain, depending on SAg).
    • Binds the lateral face of the variable β-region (Vβ) of the TCR — outside the conventional peptide-binding site.
    • SAg does NOT require antigen processing or specific peptide — acts as a "bridge" between MHC-II and TCR Vβ.
    • Activates all T cells bearing that particular Vβ family — each Vβ family is used by 2–20% of total T cells; one SAg can activate 5–30% of all T cells → massive activation.
    • T cell activation triggers CD28 co-stimulation, IL-2 production, T cell proliferation (mitogenesis).
  3. Massive cytokine release (cytokine storm)
    • T cells — IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-β, IL-4.
    • Macrophages (also activated by SAg) — IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12, IL-8.
    • Endothelial activation, capillary leak, hypotension, multi-organ dysfunction.
  4. Consequences
    • Acute — toxic shock syndrome, food poisoning (enteric form), scarlet fever, cytokine storm.
    • Chronic — T-cell anergy, deletion (activation-induced cell death — AICD), immunosuppression; contributes to autoimmune disease (Kawasaki, multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes — molecular mimicry & Vβ expansion).
    • SAgs are also implicated in staphylococcal & streptococcal toxic shock, and atopic eczema (SAg-producing S. aureus on skin).

    • Original description (1980) — menstrual TSS associated with super-absorbent tampons (Rely brand).
    • Fever >38.9 °C, hypotension (SBP <90), diffuse maculopapular rash (sunburn-like) with desquamation (especially palms & soles after 1–2 weeks), multi-organ involvement (≥3 systems): vomiting/diarrhoea, myalgia, mucous membrane hyperaemia, renal, hepatic, haematological (thrombocytopenia), CNS (altered sensorium).
    • Pathogenesis — TSST-1 crosses mucosal barrier (no digestive destruction; absorbed intact); activates T cells bearing Vβ2 (5–30%); cytokine storm (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-γ) → capillary leak, hypotension, shock, ARDS.
    • Treatment — remove source (tampon, drain abscess, debride wound); aggressive fluid resuscitation; vasopressors; clindamycin (suppresses toxin synthesis) + vancomycin/oxacillin; IVIG; admission to ICU.
    • Mortality — 3–5% with prompt treatment; 50% untreated.

2. Staphylococcal Enterotoxin B (SEB)

  • 28 kDa heat-stable protein produced by S. aureus; one of the most common causes of staphylococcal food poisoning.
  • Clinical — Food poisoning:
    • Acute onset (2–6 h after ingestion) of severe nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps; diarrhoea less prominent.
    • Self-limited (24 h); no fever; resolves without specific treatment.
    • Source — contaminated food (cream pastries, salads, dairy products, meats) left at room temperature; S. aureus grows & produces toxin.
    • Pathogenesis — SEB acts on intestinal epithelium & submucosal mast cells (via Vβ3, Vβ12, Vβ14 T cells) → local cytokine release → vomiting reflex via vagal afferents & 5-HT3 receptors on enterochromaffin cells.
    • SEB is also a bioterrorism agent (Category B) — inhalation causes severe systemic illness resembling TSS.

The defining hallmark of a superantigen is its ability to bypass antigen processing & bind directly to MHC-II outside the peptide groove + TCR Vβ outside the antigen-binding site — activating up to 30% of all T cells (vs <0.001% for conventional antigen). This explains the dramatic clinical presentations — toxic shock within hours, with high fever, hypotension, diffuse rash, multi-organ failure — and the rapid progression to death without treatment. Both respond dramatically to tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R) — the basis for its FDA approval for CRS. Bacterial superantigens are not inactivated by routine cooking — SEB survives boiling for 30 min, so reheating contaminated food does not prevent food poisoning. The implicated foods (cream pastries, mayonnaise-based salads) must be refrigerated. For suspected toxic shock, remove the source (tampon, wound packing) immediately — every minute counts.

Definitions

Definitive Host

The definitive host (final host) is the host in which the parasite reaches sexual maturity and undergoes sexual reproduction (gamete formation, fertilisation). The parasite may also multiply in the definitive host, but the defining feature is sexual maturity.

Intermediate Host

The intermediate host is the host in which the parasite undergoes asexual reproduction (larval development, metamorphosis) but does NOT reach sexual maturity. The parasite passes through one or more larval stages in the intermediate host.

Other Host-Related Terms

  • Paratenic host (transport host) — a host in which the parasite does NOT undergo any development but remains viable & accumulates, serving as a vehicle for transmission to definitive host. E.g., rodents / pigs for Trichinella (no development, accumulates in muscle).
  • Reservoir host — a host (often animal) in which the parasite lives & multiplies, serving as a continuous source of infection for humans or other hosts. E.g., dog — Echinococcus granulosus; pig — Taenia solium; cattle — Taenia saginata.
  • Vector — an arthropod that transmits the parasite from one host to another. Biological vector (parasite develops/multiplies — Anopheles for malaria) vs mechanical vector (parasite carried passively — housefly for Entamoeba).
  • Accidental / incidental host — a host not normally part of the parasite's life cycle (e.g., humans for Echinococcus — dead-end host; for Angiostrongylus).

Introduction

Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) — French chemist & microbiologist — is one of the founders of medical microbiology. His work laid the foundation for understanding microbial causation of disease, fermentation, vaccination, and aseptic practice. He pioneered the Germ Theory of Disease, displacing the prevailing theory of spontaneous generation.

Major Contributions

1. Germ Theory of Disease & Disproof of Spontaneous Generation (2 marks)

  • Pasteur demonstrated that microorganisms cause fermentation and disease — disproving the prevailing theory of spontaneous generation (held by Needham & Pouchet, that life arises de novo from non-living matter).
  • Swan-neck flask experiment (1859–64)
    • Boiled nutrient broth in flasks with long, curved (swan-neck) necks open to air.
    • Bent necks allowed air to enter but prevented dust & airborne microbes from reaching the broth.
    • Broth remained sterile indefinitely.
    • If the neck was broken or flask tipped so broth contacted dust in the neck, microbial growth appeared within days.
    • Conclusion: microbes come from other microbes (biogenesis), not spontaneous generation.
  • Pasteur's work extended the earlier work of Francesco Redi (1668 — meat & maggots) & Lazzaro Spallanzani (1765 — boiled broth in sealed flasks).
  • This work laid the foundation for Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery (1867 — carbolic acid spray), hand hygiene (Semmelweis), and modern infection control.

Pasteur's rabies vaccination of Joseph Meister (1885) is the prototype of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). His aphorism: "Chance favours only the prepared mind" — refers to his accidental discovery of chicken cholera attenuation, which led to the entire field of vaccinology. The Pasteur Institute, founded with global donations after his rabies vaccine triumph, remains a major research institution — and was where HIV-1 was first isolated in 1983 (Luc Montagnier & Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Nobel Prize 2008).
