Introduction

The WHO Five Moments for Hand Hygiene — launched in 2009 as part of the "Clean Care is Safer Care" campaign — defines the five critical moments during patient care when hand hygiene must be performed. The strategy simplifies earlier (CDC) guidelines and provides a unified, evidence-based framework for healthcare workers in all settings. It is the single most effective measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAI).

The Five Moments

Moment 1: Before touching a patient

  • When — before any physical contact with the patient (shaking hands, helping patient move, taking pulse/BP, abdominal examination, turning patient).
  • Why — protects the patient from microbes carried on the healthcare worker's hands (transient flora acquired from surfaces, other patients, environment).
  • Zone — patient zone (the patient and their immediate surroundings).
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub (preferred) or soap-and-water.

Moment 2: Before clean / aseptic procedure

  • When — before any procedure that requires aseptic technique — dressing a wound, inserting a peripheral or central venous catheter, urinary catheterisation, preparing an injection, oral care, eye care, drawing blood.
  • Why — protects the patient from microbes (including their own resident flora) entering sterile sites (bloodstream, bladder, subcutaneous tissue, wound). Most critical moment — directly prevents healthcare-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI), CAUTI, SSI.
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub; if hands visibly soiled, wash with soap & water first. For surgical procedures, surgical hand scrub with chlorhexidine/povidone-iodine (3–5 min).

Moment 3: After body fluid exposure risk

  • When — immediately after any procedure involving contact with body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin, or wound dressings — e.g., after drawing blood, changing a wound dressing, handling a used bedpan, oral suctioning, removing an IV line.
  • Why — protects the healthcare worker and the healthcare environment from microbial colonisation by patient-derived microbes (transient hand contamination).
  • Method — wash with soap & water if hands visibly soiled; otherwise alcohol-based handrub. Always remove gloves & perform hand hygiene before leaving the patient zone.

Moment 4: After touching a patient

  • When — after any physical contact with the patient (shaking hands, helping move, examination).
  • Why — protects the healthcare worker & other patients from microbes acquired from the patient.
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub or soap & water.

Moment 5: After touching patient surroundings

  • When — after contact with any inanimate object in the patient's immediate vicinity — bed rails, IV pole, bedside table, monitor, door handle, blood pressure cuff, thermometer, chart, laptop, phone.
  • Why — protects the healthcare worker & other patients from microbes left on surfaces by previous patient contact.
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub or soap & water.

Hand Hygiene Methods

Method Indication Time
Alcohol-based handrub (ABHR)Routine hand hygiene — all 5 moments (when hands not visibly soiled)20–30 sec; 3–5 mL
Soap & waterVisibly dirty hands; before eating; after toilet; suspected/confirmed C. difficile, norovirus, anthrax, spore-formers (alcohol does NOT kill spores)40–60 sec
Surgical hand scrubBefore surgical procedure2–5 min; chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine

WHO Technique — Alcohol-Based Handrub

  1. Apply enough product (3–5 mL) to cover both hands.
  2. Rub palms together.
  3. Right palm over left dorsum; left palm over right dorsum.
  4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
  5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked.
  6. Rotational rubbing of left thumb clasped in right palm & vice versa.
  7. Rotational rubbing, backwards & forwards, with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm & vice versa.
  8. Once dry, hands are safe.

Indications for Soap & Water Instead of Alcohol Handrub

  • Hands visibly soiled with blood, body fluids, dirt.
  • Before eating, after using the toilet.
  • Suspected or confirmed C. difficile infection (alcohol does not kill spores).
  • Norovirus outbreak (alcohol has limited efficacy).
  • Bacillus anthracis (spores).
  • After caring for a patient with clostridial infection.

Glove Use — Key Principles

  • Gloves are NOT a substitute for hand hygiene — they have microscopic defects and can be contaminated during removal.
  • Wear gloves when contact with blood/body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin is anticipated.
  • Change gloves between patients and between dirty & clean tasks on the same patient.
  • Remove gloves immediately after task — perform hand hygiene.
  • Do NOT wear the same pair of gloves for multiple patients.

Indications for Hand Hygiene — Beyond Five Moments

  • Before & after eating.
  • After using the toilet.
  • After coughing/sneezing into hands.
  • Before & after smoking.
  • Before putting on & after removing PPE.
  • After handling contaminated waste or laundry.

Why Hand Hygiene Saves Lives

  • Healthcare workers' hands are the most common vehicle of cross-transmission in hospitals.
  • Compliance with hand hygiene can reduce HAIs by 30–50%.
  • WHO estimates that improving hand hygiene could save 5–8 million lives annually worldwide.
  • Cost-effective — alcohol-based handrub is cheaper than soap-and-water (time, water, towels).
  • Reduces spread of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important lesson from the WHO campaign is: alcohol-based handrub is the gold standard for routine hand hygiene (20 sec, more effective, faster, better tolerated by skin, no need for water/sink/towels) — except when hands are visibly dirty or when spore-forming organisms (C. difficile, anthrax, norovirus) are suspected (then soap-and-water is mandatory because alcohol does not kill spores). The 5 Moments framework is intentionally simple — easy to remember, easy to audit, easy to teach. Compliance is monitored by direct observation (gold standard), product consumption (litres per 1000 patient-days), and increasingly by automated monitoring systems. The WHO "My 5 Moments" framework has been adopted in over 180 countries — it is the most successful patient-safety intervention in history. The rise of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (NDM, KPC, OXA-48) in Indian ICUs makes hand hygiene non-negotiable — these organisms are spread almost exclusively by contaminated hands. Wearing the same pair of gloves for multiple patients is the most dangerous hand-hygiene violation — gloves do not protect the next patient.

Definition

Enriched media are culture media that have been supplemented with additional nutrients (such as blood, serum, egg, yeast extract, haemin, vitamin K, chocolate agar) to support the growth of fastidious microorganisms — bacteria or fungi that require complex or specific growth factors and cannot grow on simple media like nutrient agar.

Fastidious organisms need growth factors such as:

  • Vitamins — NAD (V factor), hemin (X factor), vitamin K, vitamin B12, folate.
  • Amino acids, nucleotides.
  • Blood — for haemin, iron, growth factors.
  • Carbon dioxide — for capnophiles (Streptococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae).
  • Serum proteins, lipids, cholesterol.

Enriched media may be basal media supplemented with enrichments (e.g., blood agar = nutrient agar + 5–10% sheep blood), or complex defined media from the start (e.g., chocolate agar, Lowenstein-Jensen medium).

Type Function Example
Simple / basal mediumSupports non-fastidious organismsNutrient agar, peptone water
Enriched mediumSupplemented to grow fastidious organismsBlood agar, chocolate agar
Enrichment brothSelective for pathogen (inhibits competitors, favours pathogen)Selenite F broth (Salmonella), Alkaline peptone water (Vibrio)
Selective mediumContains antibiotics/chemicals that inhibit some organisms & favour othersMacConkey agar, TCBS, Lowenstein-Jensen
Differential mediumDistinguishes organisms by colour / colony morphologyMacConkey (lactose fermenter), Blood agar (haemolysis)
Transport mediumMaintains viability without multiplication during transportStuart, Cary-Blair, Amies

1. Blood Agar

  • Composition — nutrient agar base (peptone, beef extract, sodium chloride, agar, water, pH 7.2–7.6) supplemented with 5–10% defibrinated sheep/horse/human blood.
  • Why enriched — provides X factor (hemin), V factor (NAD — partially), iron, amino acids, vitamins; supports growth of fastidious organisms (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Corynebacterium, Haemophilus — partial, Listeria, enterococci, pneumococci).
  • Types
    • Sheep blood agar — preferred for streptococcal differentiation; α, β, γ haemolysis.
    • Human blood agar — less ideal (may contain antibodies, antibiotics).
    • Horse blood agar — used in UK; similar haemolysis patterns.
  • Preparation — autoclave base medium; cool to 45–50 °C; add sterile defibrinated blood (5–10%); mix gently (avoid bubbles); pour into plates; incubate at 37 °C for 24 h to check sterility.
  • Haemolysis patterns
    • α-haemolysis — partial haemolysis; greenish discolouration around colony due to oxidation of haemoglobin to methaemoglobin (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus viridans group — S. mitis, S. salivarius, S. sanguinis, S. mutans). Aerial view: green.
    • β-haemolysis — complete lysis of RBCs; clear transparent zone around colony (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae, Listeria monocytogenes — narrow; Staphylococcus aureus; Clostridium perfringens). Due to streptolysin O & S (Group A Strep), CAMP factor (Group B Strep).
    • γ-haemolysis (no haemolysis) — no change in blood agar around colony (e.g., Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus epidermidis).
  • Special tests on blood agar
    • Optochin test — differentiates S. pneumoniae (sensitive, ≥14 mm zone) from viridans streptococci (resistant).
    • Bacitracin test — differentiates S. pyogenes (sensitive) from other β-haemolytic strep.
    • CAMP test — identifies S. agalactiae (arrowhead-shaped haemolysis enhancement with Staphylococcus aureus β-lysin).
    • Satellitism test — identifies Haemophilus influenzae (grows around Staphylococcus aureus streak — provides V factor; or on nutrient agar with NAD disc).

2. Chocolate Agar

  • Composition — blood agar that has been heated to 70–80 °C after adding blood (until colour changes from red to brown — "chocolate"). Heating lyses RBCs, releasing intracellular X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD) — these are normally unavailable in unheated blood agar (V factor is intracellular in RBCs).
  • Why enriched — supports growth of more fastidious organisms than blood agar, particularly those needing both X & V factors.
  • Organisms that grow on chocolate agar but NOT blood agar
    • Haemophilus influenzae (requires X + V factor).
    • Neisseria gonorrhoeae & Neisseria meningitidis (require V factor; improved growth on chocolate agar; also need 5% CO₂ — capnophilic).
    • Moraxella catarrhalis.
  • Uses
    • Respiratory specimens — sputum for H. influenzae.
    • Genital specimens — urethral/cervical swab for N. gonorrhoeae (Thayer-Martin is selective chocolate).
    • CSF — meningitis workup (N. meningitidis, H. influenzae).
    • Eye swab — for H. influenzae biogroup aegyptius (Koch-Weeks bacillus; Brazilian purpuric fever).
  • Variants
    • Thayer-Martin medium — chocolate agar + vancomycin + colistin + nystatin (VCN inhibitor) — selective for pathogenic Neisseria; inhibits normal flora in genital/oropharyngeal specimens.
    • Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) — adds trimethoprim (VCNT).
    • New York City (NYC) medium — alternative selective medium for N. gonorrhoeae.
    • Martin-Lewis — chocolate agar + vancomycin + colistin + anisomycin.
    • GC-Lect — selective for N. gonorrhoeae.

Other Important Enriched Media (brief)

  • Loeffler's serum slope — serum + egg + glucose — for Corynebacterium diphtheriae (emphasises granules & metachromatic granules).
  • Dorset egg medium — egg yolk + saline — for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (slower than LJ).
  • Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) — egg + malachite green + glycerol + asparagine — for M. tuberculosis (selective & enriched).
  • Todd-Hewitt broth — enriched broth for Streptococcus.
  • Trypticase soy agar (TSA) / Tryptic soy broth (TSB) — general-purpose enriched medium.
  • Brain heart infusion (BHI) — enriched for fastidious organisms, yeast, mould.
  • Cooked meat broth (Robertson's) — enriched + anaerobic; for Clostridium.
  • Serum agar / serum broth — for fastidious organisms requiring serum proteins.
  • Fildes medium — peptic digest of blood; for H. influenzae.

The single most important practical lesson: chocolate agar is needed for suspected Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria infections — these organisms will not grow on blood agar (or grow poorly) because they require the V factor (NAD) which is intracellular in RBCs and only released when blood is heated. For a febrile child with meningitis, always plate CSF on both blood agar & chocolate agar (in 5% CO₂ candle jar) — and incubate overnight. Adding a chocolate agar plate to routine meningitis workup increases yield for H. influenzae and N. meningitidis dramatically. Thayer-Martin selective chocolate agar is mandatory for genital swabs in suspected gonorrhoea — non-selective chocolate agar will be overgrown by normal flora. For group A streptococcus pharyngitis, a single blood agar plate (incubated anaerobically or with 5% CO₂) is sufficient — S. pyogenes shows β-haemolysis within 24 h. Definition

Infective endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart — most commonly the heart valves (native or prosthetic), but also the mural endocardium or septum, or implanted devices (pacemaker leads, ICD).   • By acquisition — Community-acquired; Healthcare-associated (nosocomial & non-nosocomial).

  • Serology — Coxiella (phase I IgG >1:800), Bartonella henselae/quintana, Brucella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia psittaci.

  • Surgery — heart failure, uncontrolled infection (perivalvular abscess, persistent bacteraemia, fungal IE, prosthetic valve IE), large vegetations (>10 mm) with emboli, S. aureus PVE.
  • Anticoagulation — not routinely indicated; may continue for pre-existing indication.

Prevention — Antibiotic Prophylaxis

  • Indicated for high-risk cardiac conditions — prosthetic valve, previous IE, congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic; repaired with prosthetic material within 6 months; repaired with residual defect), cardiac transplant with valvulopathy, rheumatic heart disease (in endemic areas).
  • Procedures — dental (extractions, scaling); respiratory tract procedures involving incision; infected skin/musculoskeletal procedures.
  • Amoxicillin 2 g PO 30–60 min before procedure (ampicillin 2 g IV / cefazolin / clindamycin if penicillin-allergic). Not for routine GI/GU procedures.

The single most important rule for IE diagnosis is: draw 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE starting antibiotics — the diagnosis of IE rests primarily on bacteraemia documentation, not on a single positive culture. For HACEK, ask the lab to hold blood cultures for 14 days (slow grower). For suspected IE, always start with transthoracic echo (TTE), but proceed to transoesophageal echo (TOE) if TTE negative — TOE has >90% sensitivity and is essential for prosthetic valves, suspected abscess, or small vegetations. The modified Duke criteria are essential for case classification — a single major criterion (typical organism in blood culture + echo evidence of vegetation) makes the diagnosis definite. A common viva trap: S. aureus bacteraemia from any source (line infection, skin infection, IV drug use) — should always prompt echocardiography to look for IE because S. aureus has high affinity for valves and a high mortality (25–40%). Always involve cardiology, infectious disease, microbiology, and cardiac surgery early — multidisciplinary "endocarditis team" approach reduces mortality.

Definition

Fever of unknown origin (FUO) / Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) — classically defined by Petersdorf & Beeson (1961) as:

Phase 1 — Initial Workup (history, exam, basic tests)

  • Detailed history — onset, pattern, travel, occupation, animal exposure, sexual, drug, family history, transfusion, surgery, immunisation.
  • Examination — rash, lymph nodes, heart murmur, abdominal tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, joint, eye (uveitis), temporal artery (tenderness).
  • Tests — CBC, ESR, CRP, peripheral smear; LFT, RFT, electrolytes, glucose, TFT; urinalysis & urine culture; blood cultures × 3 sets; chest X-ray; HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV; Mantoux / IGRA; ECG.

  • Ferritin, iron studies (haemophagocytic syndrome).
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast — look for abscess, lymphadenopathy, malignancy.
  • Echocardiography — TTE & TOE (endocarditis).
  • Ultrasound abdomen — hepatic/renal abscess, biliary obstruction.
  • PPD / IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold).
  • Stool — culture, ova/cyst/parasite, occult blood.

  • Bone marrow aspiration & biopsy — TB, leukaemia, lymphoma, leishmaniasis.
  • Liver biopsy — granulomatous hepatitis, miliary TB, sarcoidosis, lymphoma.
  • Lymph node biopsy — TB, lymphoma, Kikuchi; excisional preferred over FNAC.
  • Temporal artery biopsy — if GCA suspected (age >50, high ESR, headache).
  • FDG-PET/CT — increasingly used in FUO; identifies occult malignancy, large-vessel vasculitis, focal infection.
  • Endoscopy — colonoscopy for IBD/malignancy; upper GI for Crohn's.
  • Surgical exploration (rare) — exploratory laparotomy (rarely done now with CT).

  • Stop unnecessary drugs — empirical withdrawal of medications (consider drug fever).
  • Document fever pattern — quotidian (single daily spike), intermittent, remittent, sustained, Pel-Ebstein (cyclical in Hodgkin).
  • Avoid empirical antibiotics, steroids, antipyretics (unless clinically unstable) — they obscure diagnosis.
  • Treat specifically once cause identified.
  • Watchful waiting if stable & diagnosis elusive — many resolve spontaneously.

Clinical Pearl

The most important rule in FUO: repeat the history & examination — repeatedly. New findings emerge over days–weeks (e.g., new murmur of endocarditis, lymphadenopathy of lymphoma, temporal artery tenderness of GCA). In Indian FUO, the three most common final diagnoses are: tuberculosis (especially extrapulmonary / miliary), enteric fever, and lymphoma — workup should focus on these. Always get an FDG-PET/CT early — it is the most useful second-line test in modern FUO workup, with sensitivity 80–90% for occult malignancy, vasculitis, and focal infection. Empirical therapy with antitubercular therapy (ATT) or steroids should be reserved for last resort — only after all diagnostic avenues exhausted or patient deteriorating. In older patients (>65 yr), giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica should always be considered — they are easily missed and respond dramatically to low-dose steroids (with temporal artery biopsy confirmation if possible). Never give empirical steroids without excluding infection — particularly TB and fungal infections which flare catastrophically. Finally, up to 25% of FUO remains undiagnosed despite extensive workup; in such patients, prognosis is generally good (~50% resolve spontaneously without sequelae).

Introduction

Escherichia coli is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, lactose-fermenting bacillus of the family Enterobacteriaceae — a normal commensal of the human gut. However, certain strains acquire virulence genes (plasmid-encoded, bacteriophage-encoded, or pathogenicity islands) that enable them to cause intestinal disease. Detailed Pathophysiology of Each Pathotype

1. ETEC — Enterotoxigenic E. coli

  • Adhesion — CFAs bind small intestinal enterocyte receptors.
  • LT (Heat-labile toxin) — AB₅ toxin similar to cholera toxin; B subunit binds GM1 ganglioside → A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gsα → ↑adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA phosphorylates CFTR → Cl⁻ secretion + inhibits NaCl absorption → secretory watery diarrhoea.
  • STa (Heat-stable toxin) — binds guanylate cyclase C receptor → ↑cGMP → PKG phosphorylates CFTR → Cl⁻ & water secretion. (STb — pig pathogen).
  • Diagnosis — PCR (LT, ST genes), bioassay (rabbit ileal loop, Y-1 adrenal cell, CHO cell, infant mouse assay); culture on MacConkey (lactose fermenter); sorbitol-MacConkey.
  • Treatment — ORS, antibiotics (rarely needed in adults; doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin); prevention — hygiene, ETEC vaccine (ETEC + cholera B subunit).

2. EPEC — Enteropathogenic E. coli

  • A/E lesion — bundle-forming pilus (BfpA) mediates initial attachment → T3SS injects Tir into enterocyte → Tir inserts into membrane → binds intimin (encoded by eae in LEE island) → tight attachment → actin polymerisation (pedestal) → microvillus effacement → malabsorption & tight junction disruption.
  • Classical — infantile diarrhoea ( outbreaks in nurseries); atypical EPEC lacks EAF plasmid but retains eae.

3. EHEC / STEC — Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli

  • Serotype O157:H7 — most common in US/Europe; non-sorbitol-fermenting (distinguishable on SMAC — sorbitol-MacConkey agar).
  • Source — undercooked beef (esp. ground beef), unpasteurised milk, contaminated water, leafy greens (spinach, lettuce), petting zoos.
  • Shiga toxin (Stx1, Stx2) — encoded by lambda-like bacteriophage; AB₅ toxin — B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on endothelial cells (especially renal glomerulus, colon) → A subunit cleaves 28S rRNA → inhibits protein synthesis → cell death. Stx2 is more associated with HUS.
  • HUS — Stx damages renal glomerular endothelium → microthrombi → MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI. Triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, AKI.
  • Diagnosis — SMAC agar (non-sorbitol fermenter), latex agglutination for O157, PCR for stx1/stx2 + eae, serotyping for non-O157 STEC (Top 6: O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, O145).
  • Treatment — supportive; avoid antibiotics (especially fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX — increase Stx release via phage induction → ↑HUS risk); avoid antimotility agents; eculizumab (anti-C5) for complement-mediated aHUS; dialysis for AKI; blood transfusion.

4. EIEC — Enteroinvasive E. coli

  • Biochemically similar to Shigella — non-motile, late/ non-lactose fermenter.
  • Invades colonic epithelial cells via M cells → escapes phagosome → multiplies in cytoplasm → spreads cell-to-cell via actin polymerisation (icsA/VirG) → mucosal ulceration → dysentery.
  • Sereny test — keratoconjunctivitis in guinea pig (invasiveness).
  • Treatment — fluoroquinolones, azithromycin; self-limiting in most.

5. EAEC — Enteroaggregative E. coli

  • Stacked-brick aggregative adherence to HEp-2 cells.
  • Biofilm formation; release of enterotoxins (EAST1, PET) → mucosal damage → persistent watery diarrhoea with mucus.
  • Germany 2011 outbreak — Shiga-toxin-producing EAEC O104:H4 — caused >4000 cases of HUS/death; sprouts as source.

6. DAEC — Diffusely adherent E. coli

  • Afa/Dr adhesins bind DAF (CD55) on enterocytes → elongation of microvilli.
  • Cause watery diarrhoea in children >12 months; sometimes UTI.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Culture — MacConkey (lactose fermenter); SMAC for O157 STEC; chromogenic agar (CHROMagar STEC).
  • Biochemical identification — TSI (A/A, gas +), IMViC (++--); Urease negative; motile (except EIEC).
  • Serotyping — O (somatic), H (flagellar), K (capsular) antigens.
  • Molecular — multiplex PCR for pathotype-specific genes (lt, st for ETEC; eae, bfpA for EPEC; stx1, stx2, eae for EHEC; ipaH, ial for EIEC; aggR, aaiC for EAEC; daaE, afa for DAEC); whole genome sequencing.
  • HEp-2 adherence assay — gold standard for EPEC (localized), EAEC (aggregative), DAEC (diffuse).
  • Bioassays — rabbit ileal loop (LT — fluid accumulation); Y-1 adrenal cell (LT — rounding); infant mouse (ST — fluid / weight ratio); Sereny test (EIEC — keratoconjunctivitis); Vero cell cytotoxicity (Stx).

Clinical Pearl

The most important clinical rule for diarrheagenic E. coli is DO NOT give antibiotics or antimotility agents in suspected EHEC/STEC (especially O157:H7) — both increase Shiga toxin release (antibiotics induce phage lysis → Stx release) and HUS risk. Antimotility agents (loperamide) prolong gut transit → more toxin absorption. Suspect EHEC in any patient with bloody diarrhoea without fever (afebrile is key — distinguishes from invasive causes like Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella which cause fever). The 2011 German outbreak of O104:H4 EAEC that acquired Stx2 gene — was initially mistaken for EHEC but was actually an enteroaggregative strain that had lysogenised the Stx2 phage — causing >4000 cases and 50 deaths; fenugreek sprouts were the source. For laboratory diagnosis, request PCR for pathotype-specific genes when clinical suspicion is high — culture alone cannot differentiate pathotypes from commensal E. coli. For traveller's diarrhoea (ETEC), self-treatment with azithromycin or rifaximin for 3 days is effective; ORS remains mainstay. For infantile EPEC in developing countries, exclusive breastfeeding (IgA protection) is the single best preventive measure.

Introduction

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) — a DNA virus of family Hepadnaviridae — causes acute and chronic hepatitis. Diagnosis & monitoring of HBV infection relies on serological markers — antigens (HBsAg, HBeAg) and antibodies (anti-HBs, anti-HBc, anti-HBe) — and molecular tests (HBV DNA PCR). Interpretation requires understanding the natural history and dynamics of these markers.

The Five Serological Markers

Marker Description Significance
HBsAg (Australia antigen)Surface antigen; appears in blood ~6 weeks post-exposure (range 1–10 weeks; before ALT rise); persists through symptomatic phaseFirst marker of infection; persistence >6 months = chronic HBV; screening test for blood donors; targets of HBV vaccine (anti-HBs antibody response)
Anti-HBs (HBsAb)Antibody to HBsAg; appears during convalescence (after HBsAg clears), ~3–6 months post-infection; persists for lifeProtective immunity marker — indicates recovery & immunity; also induced by vaccination; titre >10 mIU/mL considered protective
Anti-HBc (HBcAb)Antibody to core antigen (HBcAg is not detectable in serum as it is internalised in virion); appears early ~1–2 weeks after HBsAg; persists for lifeLifelong marker of past infection; IgM anti-HBc indicates acute infection (window period); IgG anti-HBc indicates past (resolved or chronic) infection; not induced by vaccine
HBeAgSoluble antigen derived from core; appears with or shortly after HBsAg; indicates active viral replicationMarker of high infectivity & active replication; HBeAg-positive chronic HBV has high HBV DNA; seroconversion to anti-HBe (loss of HBeAg) signals transition to inactive carrier state
Anti-HBe (HBeAb)Antibody to HBeAg; appears after HBeAg clearsSeroconversion marker — indicates reduced viral replication; but HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (with anti-HBe + HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL + ALT elevation) — precore mutant (G1896A) — still active disease

Additional Markers

  • HBV DNA (quantitative PCR) — measures viral load; appears before HBsAg (very early); used for diagnosis of acute infection (window period), monitoring chronic HBV treatment, detecting HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis, predicting HCC risk, deciding antiviral therapy (threshold >2000 IU/mL in HBeAg-negative; >20,000 IU/mL in HBeAg-positive with elevated ALT).
  • HBcAg — core antigen; not detectable in serum (internalised in Dane particle); detected in liver biopsy by immunohistochemistry.
  • HBcrAg (core-related antigen) — newer marker; reflects intrahepatic cccDNA; useful for monitoring off-treatment response.
  • HbxAg (X antigen) — research marker; involved in hepatocarcinogenesis.
  • Genotype — HBV has 10 genotypes (A–J); genotype C & D common in India; genotype predicts HBeAg seroconversion rate, treatment response (interferon — genotype A & B respond better), HCC risk.

Serological Patterns — Interpretation

HBsAg Anti-HBs Anti-HBc (IgM) Anti-HBc (IgG) HBeAg / Anti-HBe Interpretation
+–++HBeAg +Acute HBV infection (early)
+––+HBeAg + / –Chronic HBV infection (HBeAg+ or HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis)
–+–+—Resolved past infection (immune)
–+––—Vaccinated (immune; no past infection)
––+–—Window period of acute infection (or early convalescence)
–––+—Occult HBV infection (HBV DNA detectable in liver/serum despite negative HBsAg) — low infectivity; may reactivate with immunosuppression
++–+—Chronic HBV with escape mutation (HBsAg mutant; anti-HBs not protective) OR resolving infection with coexisting antigen & antibody

Window Period

The gap between HBsAg disappearance and anti-HBs appearance (~2–6 weeks); anti-HBc IgM is the only marker present — diagnostic of acute HBV. Modern HBsAg assays (CMIA, ECLIA) have shortened the window by detecting HBsAg at very low levels (~0.05 IU/mL); HBV DNA PCR can detect infection even earlier (~1 week post-exposure).

Chronic HBV — Phases (based on HBeAg & ALT)

  1. Immune tolerant phase — HBeAg+, high HBV DNA (>10⁷ IU/mL), normal ALT, minimal liver disease; common in perinatally acquired HBV; lasts decades.
  2. Immune active HBeAg+ phase — HBeAg+, high HBV DNA, elevated ALT, active hepatitis; may progress to cirrhosis/HCC.
  3. Inactive carrier phase — HBeAg–, anti-HBe+, low HBV DNA (<2000 IU/mL), normal ALT; no active liver disease; stable for years.
  4. HBeAg-negative immune active phase — HBeAg–, anti-HBe+, HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, elevated ALT; precore (G1896A) or basal core promoter (A1762T/G1764A) mutants; common in Asia & Mediterranean.
  5. HBsAg clearance / resolved — HBsAg disappears, anti-HBs develops; very low HCC risk.

Antiviral Treatment

  • Indications — HBeAg+ with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL + ALT ≥2× ULN; HBeAg– with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL + ALT ≥2× ULN; cirrhosis with detectable HBV DNA; immunosuppression (prophylaxis); pregnancy (TDF to prevent vertical transmission if HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL).
  • First-line — Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) 300 mg OD or Entecavir 0.5–1 mg OD; pegylated interferon alfa-2a (limited use — weekly SC × 48 weeks).
  • Duration — HBeAg+ : until HBeAg seroconversion + 12 months consolidation; HBeAg– : indefinite; cirrhosis: indefinite.
  • Monitoring — HBV DNA every 3–6 months; ALT; HBeAg/anti-HBe annually; HBsAg annually; ultrasound + AFP every 6 months for HCC surveillance (high-risk).

Prevention

  • Hepatitis B vaccine — recombinant HBsAg (yeast-derived); 3 doses at 0, 1, 6 months; intramuscular (deltoid); induces anti-HBs; protective titre >10 mIU/mL; >95% seroprotection in adults.
  • Universal immunisation — birth dose within 24 h (especially in HBV-endemic countries to prevent vertical transmission), then 6, 10, 14 weeks (EPI schedule).
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis — HBIG (hepatitis B immune globulin) 0.06 mL/kg IM within 24 h (preferably <12 h) + vaccine series; for needle-stick, sexual, perinatal exposure.
  • Perinatal transmission — HBsAg-positive mothers: HBIG + vaccine at birth; TDF in third trimester if high viral load (≥200,000 IU/mL) — reduces vertical transmission to <1%.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical use of HBV markers is to distinguish between acute infection, chronic infection, resolved past infection, and vaccine-induced immunity — each has a unique serological profile. A simple rule: isolated anti-HBs = vaccinated; anti-HBc (IgG) + anti-HBs = past infection resolved; HBsAg + anti-HBc (IgG) = chronic infection; anti-HBc (IgM) alone = acute infection in window period. For blood donor screening, only HBsAg is used in many countries — but in low-prevalence areas with high vaccination rates, anti-HBc is added to detect occult HBV infection. HBV DNA PCR is now considered the gold standard for detecting infection during the window period, occult HBV, and monitoring antiviral therapy. The most important advance in chronic HBV management is the recognition of HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (precore mutant) — these patients have normal HBeAg but high HBV DNA & active hepatitis, and require treatment. Always check HBV status before starting chemotherapy, biological therapy, or rituximab — HBV reactivation (especially in HBsAg+ / anti-HBc+ patients) causes fatal hepatitis in up to 50%; prophylactic TDF/entecavir must be given throughout immunosuppression and for 12–18 months after.

Definition

Food poisoning (food-borne illness) is an acute illness caused by consumption of food contaminated with pathogenic microorganisms, their toxins, or chemicals — presenting typically with gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea) within hours to days of ingestion. The pattern of symptoms, incubation period, and food source help identify the cause.

Classification

A. Infectious Food Poisoning (microbial invasion of gut)

  • Caused by ingestion of live pathogens which multiply in the gut and invade mucosa.
  • Longer incubation (12–72 h); fever often present; inflammatory diarrhoea (blood/pus) common.

B. Toxic / Intoxicating Food Poisoning (preformed toxin ingestion)

  • Caused by ingestion of preformed toxin produced by microbes growing in food.
  • Short incubation (1–6 h); vomiting prominent; usually no fever; non-inflammatory.

C. Toxicoinfectious Food Poisoning

  • Pathogens ingested in food, multiply in gut, then produce toxin in vivo.
  • Intermediate incubation (6–24 h); watery diarrhoea.

D. Non-bacterial / chemical / parasitic / plant / marine food poisoning

Important Causes — Detailed

1. Staphylococcal Food Poisoning (Toxic)

  • Cause — enterotoxins A, B, C1, C2, C3, D, E, G–U produced by Staphylococcus aureus; superantigen activity.
  • Source — contaminated food handler (carrier with S. aureus on hands, nasal discharge); cream pastries, mayonnaise, salads (egg, tuna, chicken), dairy products, ham, custard. Food left at room temperature allows S. aureus growth & toxin production.
  • Incubation — 1–6 h (rapid).
  • Symptoms — sudden severe nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps; diarrhoea less prominent; no fever.
  • Duration — <24 h; self-limiting.
  • Diagnosis — culture food for S. aureus (coagulase +); phage typing; enterotoxin detection by ELISA/PCR.
  • Treatment — supportive (fluids, antiemetics); no antibiotics.

2. Bacillus cereus Food Poisoning (Toxic — 2 types)

  • Type 1 — Emetic type
    • Cause — cereulide (a small cyclic peptide toxin, heat-stable, acid-stable) preformed in food.
    • Source — fried rice (Chinese restaurant rice — held warm for hours), pasta, pastries.
    • Incubation — 1–6 h; resembles staphylococcal food poisoning.
    • Symptoms — nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps; diarrhoea less common; no fever.
    • Duration — <24 h.
  • Type 2 — Diarrhoeal type
    • Cause — heat-labile enterotoxin (similar to E. coli LT or cholera toxin) produced in gut after ingestion.
    • Source — meats, vegetables, sauces.
    • Incubation — 6–24 h.
    • Symptoms — watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; vomiting less prominent.
    • Duration — <24 h.
  • Diagnosis — culture food for B. cereus (spore-forming Gram-positive bacillus).

3. Clostridium perfringens Food Poisoning (Toxicoinfectious)

  • Cause — Type A strain of C. perfringens produces enterotoxin (CPE) in gut after sporulation; CPE binds tight junction → capillary permeability & fluid secretion.
  • Source — meat, poultry, stews, gravies cooked in bulk & left at room temperature (allows spore germination & multiplication).
  • Incubation — 8–16 h.
  • Symptoms — watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; vomiting rare; no fever.
  • Duration — 24 h.
  • C. perfringens type C — causes necrotising enteritis ("Pig-bel" — Papua New Guinea after pork feasts).

4. Botulism — Clostridium botulinum (Toxic)

  • Cause — preformed neurotoxin (A, B, E most common) in food; blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction.
  • Source — home-canned vegetables, fruits, meats; preserved fish (type E); honey in infants.
  • Incubation — 12–36 h (up to several days).
  • Symptoms — descending flaccid paralysis; cranial nerves first — diplopia, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, blurred vision; symmetric motor paralysis; respiratory failure; NO fever; no sensory loss.
  • Diagnosis — toxin in food, serum, stool (mouse bioassay, PCR).
  • Treatment — trivalent equine botulinum antitoxin (A, B, E) ASAP; respiratory support; no aminoglycosides (worsen paralysis).

5. Salmonella Food Poisoning (Infectious — Salmonella gastroenteritis)

  • Cause — non-typhoidal Salmonella — S. Enteritidis, S. Typhimurium, S. Newport; invasive infection of ileum & colon.
  • Source — poultry, eggs, meat, milk, reptiles (pets).
  • Incubation — 12–72 h.
  • Symptoms — diarrhoea (may be bloody), fever, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting.
  • Duration — 4–7 days.
  • Diagnosis — stool culture on MacConkey, XLD, DCA; serotyping.
  • Treatment — supportive (ORS); antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone) only for severe disease, immunocompromised, infants <3 months, elderly, sickle cell disease.

6. Shigella Food Poisoning (Infectious — bacillary dysentery)

  • Cause — Shigella spp.; low infective dose (~10 organisms).
  • Source — contaminated food/water; person-to-person faecal-oral.
  • Incubation — 1–3 days.
  • Symptoms — bloody mucoid diarrhoea, fever, abdominal cramps, tenesmus; HUS in S. dysenteriae type 1.
  • Treatment — ciprofloxacin, azithromycin; avoid antimotility.

7. Campylobacter jejuni (Infectious)

  • Source — poultry, unpasteurised milk, water; pets.
  • Incubation — 2–5 days.
  • Symptoms — diarrhoea (often bloody), fever, abdominal pain (may mimic appendicitis); Guillain-Barré syndrome (rare — antiganglioside antibody).
  • Diagnosis — stool culture on Skirrow/Campylobacter blood agar at 42 °C microaerophilic.

8. E. coli Food Poisoning (Toxicoinfectious / Infectious)

  • ETEC — traveller's diarrhoea (watery); EHEC O157:H7 — bloody diarrhoea, HUS; EIEC — dysentery-like; EPEC — infantile diarrhoea; EAEC — persistent diarrhoea.
  • Source — contaminated water, food (beef for EHEC; salads, fruits, water for ETEC).
  • Incubation — 1–10 days (varies).

9. Vibrio parahaemolyticus

  • Marine bacterium; from seafood (raw oysters, sushi, shellfish); coastal outbreaks.
  • Incubation — 12–24 h; watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps; self-limiting in 3 days.

10. Vibrio cholerae — Cholera (Toxicoinfectious)

  • Watery rice-water stools; massive dehydration; contaminated water.
  • Incubation — few hours to 5 days.

11. Listeria monocytogenes

  • From unpasteurised dairy, soft cheese, deli meats, smoked fish; replicates at 4 °C (refrigerator).
  • Incubation — 1–4 weeks (longer than most).
  • Symptoms — flu-like, gastroenteritis; invasive disease — meningitis, septicaemia, abortion in pregnancy, neonatal listeriosis.

12. Yersinia enterocolitica

  • From pork, milk, water; replicates at 4 °C.
  • Incubation — 1–7 days; fever, abdominal pain (pseudo-appendicitis due to mesenteric adenitis), diarrhoea; reactive arthritis.

13. Viral Food Poisoning

  • Norovirus — "cruise ship gastroenteritis"; rapid onset (12–48 h); vomiting prominent; watery diarrhoea; self-limiting in 1–3 days.
  • Hepatitis A virus — food-borne (shellfish, berries, salad); incubation 15–50 days.
  • Rotavirus — infantile gastroenteritis.

14. Parasitic Food Poisoning

  • Giardia lamblia — contaminated water; bloating, foul-smelling stools.
  • Cryptosporidium — watery diarrhoea, especially HIV.
  • Entamoeba histolytica — amoebic dysentery.
  • Trichinella spiralis — undercooked pork; myalgia, periorbital oedema.
  • Taenia solium/saginata — undercooked pork/beef; cysticercosis.
  • Anisakis — raw fish sushi; gastric pain.

15. Non-bacterial Food Poisoning

  • Chemical — heavy metals (arsenic, mercury, lead); pesticides (organophosphates — cholinergic crisis); MSG (Chinese restaurant syndrome); contaminants.
  • Plant toxins — cyanogenic glycosides (cassava); solanine (green potatoes); ricin (castor beans); muscarine (Inocybe mushrooms); amatoxin (Amanita phalloides — delayed hepatotoxicity); aflatoxin (Aspergillus — peanuts).
  • Marine toxins
    • Ciguatera — dinoflagellate toxin in reef fish (barracuda, grouper, snapper); GI + neuro (temperature reversal — hot/cold reversal) + cardiovascular.
    • Paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP) — saxitoxin from dinoflagellates in shellfish; rapid paralysis.
    • Scombroid — histamine from spoiled dark-meat fish (tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi); flushing, urticaria, headache, resembles allergy; treated with antihistamines.
    • Tetrodotoxin — pufferfish (fugu); potent neurotoxin blocking Na+ channels; high mortality.

Clinical Pearl

The incubation period is the single most useful clue to the cause of food poisoning: <6 h — preformed toxin (S. aureus, B. cereus emetic, heavy metals); 8–16 h — Clostridium perfringens, B. cereus diarrhoeal; 12–72 h — infectious (Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter, Norovirus, Vibrio); >1 week — Listeria, Yersinia, hepatitis A, Giardia. The food source narrows the differential: undercooked ground beef → EHEC O157:H7 (consider HUS); fried rice → B. cereus; chicken → Salmonella, Campylobacter; raw seafood → Vibrio, Norovirus, Hepatitis A, Anisakis; unpasteurised milk → Listeria, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Brucella; home-canned vegetables → C. botulinum. Always report food poisoning outbreaks to public health authorities — to enable source tracing & prevent further cases. For suspected HUS in a child with bloody diarrhoea, send stool for EHEC O157:H7 culture (SMAC) and Shiga toxin PCR — and avoid antibiotics. The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food (keep clean; separate raw & cooked; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water & raw materials) is the most effective public health intervention.

Definition

Empathy is the capacity to understand, appreciate, and share the emotional experience, perspective, and feelings of another person — without losing one's own sense of self — and to communicate this understanding back to them in a caring, non-judgmental way. It is the cornerstone of the doctor-patient relationship and a core competency in medical practice.

Empathy differs from:

  • Sympathy — feeling for someone (pity, sorrow); an emotional reaction rather than cognitive understanding.
  • Compassion — empathy + a desire to relieve suffering (action-oriented).
  • Pity — feeling sorry without deep understanding; can be condescending.
  • Identification / projection — confusing one's own feelings with the patient's.

Components of Empathy

  1. Cognitive empathy — understanding the patient's perspective, thoughts, and concerns ("I can see how this must look from where you stand").
  2. Affective (emotional) empathy — sharing the emotional experience ("I can feel how frightening this must be").
  3. Behavioural empathy — communicating understanding through words, tone, body language, active listening, eye contact, and therapeutic action ("Let's sit down together and work through this").

Why Empathy Matters in Patient Care (4 marks)

1. Improves Clinical Outcomes

  • Better diagnostic accuracy — patients disclose symptoms, concerns, and lifestyle factors more completely to empathic doctors; reduces missing information (history-taking).
  • Improved adherence to treatment — patients follow recommendations when they feel understood & respected; medication adherence rates are 19% higher with empathic clinicians.
  • Better symptom control — chronic disease outcomes (diabetes, hypertension, asthma, cancer) improve; HbA1c reduction of 0.5–1% in empathic doctor-patient dyads.
  • Reduced complications — earlier reporting of side effects; fewer hospitalisations; shorter length of stay.
  • Placebo / nocebo effects amplified — empathic interactions enhance the therapeutic ritual, improving clinical benefit even beyond pharmacology.

2. Enhances Patient Satisfaction & Trust

  • Patients rate empathic clinicians higher on satisfaction surveys.
  • Builds therapeutic alliance — patients feel heard, respected, and partners in decision-making.
  • Increases likelihood of returning for follow-up & preventive care.
  • Reduces patient complaints, grievances, and medico-legal litigation — studies show a 50% reduction in malpractice claims in clinicians with high empathy scores.

3. Reduces Patient Suffering & Anxiety

  • Validates the patient's emotional experience — reduces sense of isolation.
  • Softens the impact of bad news (cancer diagnosis, terminal illness, death of loved one).
  • Helps patients cope with chronic illness, pain, disability, and end-of-life decisions.
  • Decreases anxiety, depression, and psychological distress — measurable reduction in cortisol, blood pressure, and pain scores after empathic interactions.

4. Improves Communication & Cultural Competence

  • Bridges language, cultural, socioeconomic, and educational gaps.
  • Encourages open dialogue — patients ask questions, express concerns, disclose sensitive information (sexual history, substance use, domestic violence).
  • Supports shared decision-making — patient-centred care, autonomy, informed consent.
  • Helps navigate ethical dilemmas — end-of-life, withdrawal of treatment, futile care.

5. Reduces Burnout in Doctors

  • Counterintuitively, empathic engagement (when balanced with self-care) reduces rather than increases physician burnout.
  • Provides meaning & professional satisfaction — reconnects doctors with the humanistic core of medicine.
  • Empathy training in medical schools improves resilience and reduces depersonalisation.
  • Compassion fatigue — occurs when emotional empathy is unbalanced by self-care; need for self-awareness, boundaries, and reflective practice.

6. Strengthened Doctor-Patient Relationship

  • Builds trust, rapport, and confidence over time.
  • Encourages patient loyalty — patients return to clinicians who treat them with humanity.
  • Creates therapeutic environment — the "healing relationship" is itself a treatment.
  • Facilitates difficult conversations — breaking bad news (SPIKES protocol), discussing code status, advance directives.

How to Demonstrate Empathy in Clinical Practice

  1. Active listening — full attention; no interruption; let the patient complete their narrative; allow silence.
  2. Eye contact & open body language — sit at patient's level, lean slightly forward, uncrossed arms; reduce barriers (computer screen, desk).
  3. Reflective statements — paraphrase what the patient said: "What I'm hearing is that the pain has been worse for the past week and you're worried it might be cancer."
  4. Acknowledge emotions — "This must be very difficult for you." "I can see how frightened you are."
  5. Validate feelings — "It's completely understandable that you feel angry after hearing this diagnosis."
  6. Use the NURSE acronym — Naming ("It sounds like you're frustrated"), Understanding ("I can understand why"), Respecting ("You've been very brave"), Supporting ("I'll be with you through this"), Exploring ("Tell me more about what worries you").
  7. Open-ended questions — "What brings you here today?" "What are you most concerned about?"
  8. Non-verbal cues — nodding, facial expressions matching the patient's emotion, hand on shoulder (when culturally appropriate).
  9. Cultural humility — ask about patient's beliefs, values, preferences, family role in decision-making.
  10. Time & presence — even brief empathic moments (90 seconds) can transform a consultation.

Empathy in Specific Clinical Situations

  • Breaking bad news — SPIKES protocol (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy/Summary). Empathy is the bridge between delivering facts and supporting the patient emotionally.
  • End-of-life discussions — empathic exploration of fears, hopes, values, spiritual beliefs; supports dignity therapy.
  • Palliative & hospice care — empathy is the core skill; relieves existential suffering.
  • Psychiatry — therapeutic alliance; validation; understanding delusions/hallucinations from patient's perspective.
  • Paediatrics — engaging with both child & parent; reassurance; play.
  • Difficult patients — empathy for underlying fear, pain, addiction, personality disorder — de-escalates.

Clinical Pearl

Empathy is not a soft skill — it is a hard clinical skill with measurable effects on outcomes, adherence, satisfaction, and litigation. The Jefferson Scale of Empathy (JSE) — developed by Dr. Mohammadreza Hojat at Jefferson Medical College — quantifies empathy in medical students & physicians; higher JSE scores correlate with better clinical outcomes and lower patient complaints. The single most powerful empathy statement — "I wish I had better news for you" — costs nothing but transforms the doctor-patient relationship. Empathy can be taught & cultivated — through communication skills training, narrative medicine, role-play, patient shadowing, reflective journaling, and Balint groups. The Bangalore & St. John's narrative medicine programs in India have shown that brief empathy training improves both patient outcomes and physician well-being. Compassion fatigue — emotional exhaustion from sustained empathic engagement — is the price of empathy; mitigate through self-care, peer support, supervision, mindfulness, and boundary setting. Sir William Osler's aphorism: "It is much more important to know what sort of a patient has a disease than what sort of a disease a patient has." Empathy is the bridge between these two.

Introduction

Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) is an acute invasive enteric infection caused by Shigella species — Gram-negative, non-motile, non-lactose-fermenting bacilli of family Enterobacteriaceae. Despite a low infective dose (~10–100 organisms), it causes worldwide morbidity & mortality, especially in children <5 years in developing countries.

Classification

Species Serogroup Serotypes Epidemiology
S. dysenteriaeA15 serotypes; type 1 most virulentEpidemic; severe; produces Shiga toxin; HUS risk; India, Africa, SE Asia
S. flexneriB14 serotypes; 2a most commonMost common in developing countries (India, Asia); endemic; moderate severity
S. boydiiC20 serotypesIndian subcontinent; rare elsewhere; moderate
S. sonneiD1 serotype (form I & II)Most common in developed countries; mild; emerging in India

Pathogenesis (3 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Reservoir — humans only (no animal reservoir). Cases & asymptomatic carriers.
  • Transmission — faecal-oral; contaminated water & food; person-to-person (low infective dose, ~10–100 bacilli); flies (vector). Houseflies can transmit Shigella from faeces to food.
  • Incubation period — 1–3 days (range 12 h–7 days).
  • Low infective dose — Shigella survives gastric acid (acid-tolerant); explains high transmissibility & outbreaks in day-care centres, mental institutions, refugee camps.

2. Invasion of Colonic Mucosa

  1. Entry via M cells of Peyer's patches in ileum & colon — Shigella does not invade enterocytes directly; instead it is taken up by M cells overlying lymphoid follicles.
  2. Transcytosis & release to macrophages — Shigella is released into the subepithelial dome, phagocytosed by macrophages.
  3. Macrophage apoptosis — Shigella escapes the phagosome via IpaB (T3SS effector) → induces caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis → releases IL-1β & IL-18 → recruits neutrophils.
  4. Basolateral invasion of enterocytes — Shigella invades colonic enterocytes from the basolateral side (not apical) via membrane ruffling induced by T3SS effectors (IpaA, IpaC, IpgB1, SopE) — triggers actin polymerisation & macropinocytosis.
  5. Intracellular multiplication — Shigella escapes phagosome (IpaB lyses vacuole), multiplies in cytoplasm.
  6. Cell-to-cell spread — IcsA (VirG) polymerises actin at one pole of bacterium → "actin tail" propels bacterium through cytoplasm → pushes against cell membrane → forms protrusion into adjacent enterocyte → double-membrane vacuole → lysis → cycle repeats. This allows spread without extracellular exposure — escapes immune system.

3. Toxin Production

  • Shiga toxin (Stx) — produced only by S. dysenteriae type 1; AB₅ toxin similar to EHEC Stx.
    • B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on endothelial cells (especially renal glomerulus, colon).
    • A subunit cleaves 28S rRNA → inhibits protein synthesis → cell death.
    • Cytotoxic to colonic epithelium (haemorrhagic colitis) & renal endothelium → haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS).
    • Also has enterotoxic effect — secretory diarrhoea in early illness.
    • Neurotoxic effect — seizures in children.
  • Shigella enterotoxins (ShET1, ShET2) — chromosomal/plasmid-encoded; secretory watery diarrhoea in early phase.
  • Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin — fever, inflammation, septic shock.

4. Inflammatory Response & Ulcer Formation

  • IL-1β, IL-8, TNF-α recruit neutrophils → intense acute inflammation of colonic mucosa.
  • Neutrophils release proteases & ROS → mucosal destruction → ulceration (superficial ulcers with elevated margins).
  • Pseudomembrane formation (fibrin, mucus, neutrophils, necrotic epithelium) — like pseudomembranous colitis.
  • Hyperaemia, oedema, haemorrhage → bloody mucoid diarrhoea ("red currant jelly" stool).
  • Healing by regeneration — usually no scarring (unlike TB).

5. Pathology

  • Site — sigmoid colon & rectum (most severe); may extend proximally to entire colon; terminal ileum occasionally.
  • Macroscopy — mucosa hyperaemic, oedematous, friable; superficial ulcers with elevated margins; pseudomembrane.
  • Microscopy — acute non-specific inflammation; neutrophil infiltrate; crypt abscesses; mucosal ulceration; pseudomembrane (fibrinopurulent exudate). Granulomas absent (distinguishes from Crohn's, TB).

Clinical Features

  • Acute onset fever, malaise, anorexia, abdominal cramps.
  • Diarrhoea — initially watery, then bloody mucoid (dysentery) within 24–48 h.
  • Tenesmus, rectal pain, urgency.
  • Stool frequency 10–30+ per day, small volume.
  • Dehydration in severe cases.
  • Children — seizures (Shiga toxin neurotoxicity, fever, hyponatraemia).
  • Resolves in 5–7 days (untreated) without carrier state.

Complications

  • Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — S. dysenteriae type 1 (Shiga toxin).
  • Intestinal perforation — rare; toxic megacolon.
  • Rectal prolapse — children with severe tenesmus.
  • Reactive arthritis / Reiter syndrome — HLA-B27; asymmetric oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis (after S. flexneri).
  • Bacteraemia — rare (immunocompromised, malnourished children).
  • Seizures — children (neurotoxicity).
  • Hyponatraemia — SIADH-like, especially in children.
  • Leukaemoid reaction — WBC >50,000/µL in severe S. dysenteriae type 1 infection.
  • Post-dysenteric irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Laboratory Diagnosis (3 marks)

1. Specimen Collection

  • Fresh stool or rectal swab (Cary-Blair transport) — collected early in illness (before antibiotics); mucus flakes / blood-tinged portion preferred.
  • Multiple samples (3) increase yield.
  • Transport rapidly — Shigella is fragile; survives only briefly outside gut.

2. Macroscopic & Microscopic Examination

  • Gross — stool scanty, mucoid, blood-tinged, purulent; alkaline.
  • Microscopy
    • Saline mount — numerous pus cells (sheets), RBCs (discrete), macrophages.
    • Gram stain — Gram-negative bacilli; few normal flora (less than typical stool).
    • No amoebic trophozoites (distinguishes from amoebic dysentery).
  • Occult blood — positive.
  • pH — alkaline (>7).

3. Culture

  • Selective media
    • MacConkey agar — Shigella appears as non-lactose-fermenting (colourless) colonies; differentiates from E. coli (pink).
    • XLD (Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate) agar — Shigella appears as red colonies (non-xylose-fermenting); Salmonella is black (H₂S+).
    • SS (Salmonella-Shigella) agar — selective for both Salmonella & Shigella; Shigella = colourless colonies.
    • DC (Deoxycholate Citrate) agar.
    • Gram-negative broth (GN) — enrichment (incubated 4–6 h, then subcultured).
  • Incubation — 37 °C for 24 h aerobic (Shigella is facultative anaerobe).

4. Identification

Test Shigella result
Gram stainGram-negative bacillus, non-spore-forming
MotilityNon-motile (no H antigen) — distinguishes from Salmonella, E. coli
Lactose fermentationNon-lactose-fermenter (late lactose fermenter in some S. sonnei)
TSIAlkaline slant / acid butt (KA); no gas; no H₂S (distinguishes from Salmonella — K/A gas+ H₂S+)
UreaseNegative
CitrateNegative
Lysine decarboxylaseNegative

5. Serotyping (Slide Agglutination)

  • Polyvalent antisera for groups A, B, C, D.
  • Then monovalent antisera for serotype (within group).
  • S. dysenteriae — Group A antisera (10 types); S. flexneri — Group B (6 types); S. boydii — Group C (15 types); S. sonnei — Group D (single type, phase I & II).

6. Molecular Tests

  • PCR — ipaH gene (multi-copy, chromosomal & plasmid — most sensitive); ial (invasion-associated locus); virA; stxA (Shiga toxin for S. dysenteriae type 1); wbgZ (S. sonnei); ply.
  • Multiplex PCR — distinguishes Shigella from EIEC (both have ipaH; differentiate by other targets).
  • Real-time PCR — rapid; useful in outbreak investigation.
  • WGS — typing for epidemiology; PulseNet.

7. Antimicrobial Susceptibility

  • Important — Shigella has rapidly developed resistance; most strains now resistant to cotrimoxazole, ampicillin, tetracycline, nalidixic acid; emerging fluoroquinolone resistance (especially in India, Asia).
  • Currently recommended first-line (WHO): ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 3 days (or azithromycin 500 mg OD × 3 days; ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 5 days for severe or resistant cases); pivmecillinam.
  • Always send stool for culture & sensitivity before starting antibiotics — but do not delay empirical treatment in severe cases.

8. Other Tests

  • Blood culture — rare bacteraemia; in immunocompromised.
  • Sigmoidoscopy — diffuse mucosal inflammation, friability, superficial ulcers (typically rectosigmoid); biopsy for histology (acute non-specific inflammation).
  • Sereny test — keratoconjunctivitis in guinea pig (invasiveness) — historical.
  • Cell culture invasion assay — HeLa, HEp-2 cells (invasiveness).

Treatment

  • Rehydration — ORS (WHO formula) for mild–moderate; IV fluids for severe.
  • Antibiotics — shorten illness duration & pathogen excretion; recommended in severe disease, dysentery, infants, immunocompromised; ciprofloxacin (or azithromycin, ceftriaxone in pregnancy & children).
  • Zinc supplementation — children <5 yr (reduces duration & severity).
  • Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) — prolongs pathogen contact & toxin absorption; risk of toxic megacolon, HUS.
  • Avoid opioids, NSAIDs.

Prevention

  • Safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene, food safety, fly control.
  • Outbreak investigation & reporting.
  • No licensed vaccine widely available; candidate vaccines — conjugate (S. flexneri 2a, S. sonnei — Shigella O-specific polysaccharide conjugated to tetanus toxoid, ETEC-Shigella hybrid); live attenuated oral (Flexyn2a, WRSS1, WRSs3).

Clinical Pearl

The most important clinical rule for shigellosis is: always consider Shigella in any patient with acute bloody mucoid diarrhoea + fever + tenesmus — especially children <5 yr in India, where S. flexneri is the dominant serogroup. The single best laboratory test is stool culture on MacConkey + XLD or SS agar — Shigella appears as non-lactose-fermenting, non-motile colonies (TSI: K/A, no gas, no H₂S). Always send stool culture & sensitivity — because resistance to fluoroquinolones and azithromycin is rising rapidly in India, and antibiotic choice should be guided by local antibiogram. The most feared complication is HUS in S. dysenteriae type 1 infection — caused by Shiga toxin (similar to EHEC O157:H7); watch for falling platelets, rising creatinine, schistocytes on blood smear, and avoid antibiotics in suspected S. dysenteriae type 1 (may increase toxin release via phage induction — same caution as EHEC). Always avoid antimotility agents — they worsen dysentery & increase HUS risk. For children, give zinc supplementation along with ORS — proven mortality benefit. Public health measures (water, sanitation, hygiene — "WASH") are the most effective long-term prevention.

Introduction

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral infection caused by dengue virus (DENV, serotypes 1–4) of family Flaviviridae, transmitted by Aedes aegypti (primary) and Aedes albopictus (secondary). The World Health Organization (WHO 2009, updated 2012) classification guides clinical management — dengue has a wide clinical spectrum from asymptomatic to severe life-threatening illness.

WHO 2009 Classification (3 marks)

1. Dengue without Warning Signs (previously "DF" — Dengue Fever)

  • Clinical — acute high fever (typically biphasic/saddleback, 2–7 days); two of: headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, rash, haemorrhagic manifestations (petechiae, positive tourniquet test), leucopenia.
  • Lab — positive tourniquet test, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, rising haematocrit (5–10%).
  • No plasma leakage; no organ impairment.
  • Usually self-limiting; recovery in 5–7 days.

2. Dengue with Warning Signs

  • Dengue without warning signs + any of the following warning signs:
  • Abdominal pain or tenderness.
  • Persistent vomiting (≥3 times/day) or vomiting without relief.
  • Clinical fluid accumulation — pleural effusion, ascites.
  • Mucosal bleeding — gums, nose, GIT, menorrhagia.
  • Lethargy, restlessness or somnolence.
  • Hepatomegaly >2 cm.
  • Laboratory — increasing haematocrit with rapid decline in platelet count.
  • Requires hospitalisation for close monitoring; may progress to severe dengue during the critical phase (defervescence, day 3–7 of illness).

3. Severe Dengue (previously DHF/DSS — Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever / Dengue Shock Syndrome)

Defined by one or more of the following:

  1. Severe plasma leakage leading to:
    • Dengue shock syndrome (DSS) — pulse pressure ≤20 mmHg with weak/undetectable pulse, hypotension, cold clammy extremities, capillary refill >3 sec, restlessness; or
    • Fluid accumulation with respiratory distress (massive pleural effusion, ascites).
  2. Severe haemorrhage — severe mucosal bleeding, haematemesis, melaena, menorrhagia, intracranial bleed, haemothorax; Hess test (tourniquet) strongly positive; severe thrombocytopenia.
  3. Severe organ involvement
    • Hepatitis — AST/ALT ≥1000 IU/L.
    • Encephalitis / encephalopathy — impaired consciousness, seizures.
    • Myocarditis, cardiogenic shock.
    • Acute kidney injury.
    • ARDS.

Laboratory Criteria for Severe Dengue

  • Platelet count <100,000/µL.
  • Haematocrit rise ≥20% from baseline (indicates plasma leakage).
  • Hypoalbuminaemia, hypoproteinaemia.
  • Rising haematocrit + falling platelet count = impending shock.
  • Positive tourniquet test (>20 petechiae per square inch).
  • Pleural effusion on chest X-ray (right-sided commonly).
  • Ultrasound — gallbladder wall thickening, ascites, pleural effusion.

Phases of Dengue Illness

  1. Febrile phase (days 1–3) — high fever, headache, myalgia, rash; may have haemorrhagic manifestations.
  2. Critical phase (days 3–7, around defervescence) — plasma leakage; lasts 24–48 h; watch for shock.
  3. Recovery phase (days 7–10) — reabsorption of fluid; haematocrit falls, platelets rise, bradycardia, pruritic confluent erythematous rash with "isles of white in sea of red".

Pathophysiology of Severe Dengue

  • Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) — secondary infection with different serotype; pre-existing non-neutralising antibodies form immune complexes → increased viral uptake by Fc-receptor-bearing monocytes/macrophages → massive viral replication → cytokine storm (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, IFN-γ, MCP-1).
  • Complement activation → C5a, C3a → increased vascular permeability.
  • Capillary leak → plasma escapes into interstitial space (pleural, peritoneal) → hypovolaemia, shock.
  • Bone marrow suppression → thrombocytopenia; platelet dysfunction → bleeding.
  • hepatic dysfunction → transaminitis, jaundice.

Older WHO 1997 Classification (still used in some regions)

  • Undifferentiated fever.
  • Dengue fever (DF).
  • Dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) grades I–IV
    • Grade I — fever + non-specific symptoms; positive tourniquet test only.
    • Grade II — grade I + spontaneous bleeding (skin, gums, nose, GIT).
    • Grade III — circulatory failure (weak pulse, narrow pulse pressure ≤20 mmHg, hypotension, cold clammy skin, restlessness).
    • Grade IV — profound shock (undetectable BP, pulse).
    Grades III & IV = DSS (Dengue Shock Syndrome).

Diagnosis

  • NS1 antigen ELISA — first 1–5 days (sensitivity 90% in first 3 days).
  • IgM ELISA — appears day 4–5; peaks at 2 weeks; persists 3 months.
  • IgG ELISA — rises later; persists for life; high IgG + IgM = secondary infection.
  • RT-PCR — early (first 5 days); detects viral RNA & serotype.
  • Viral isolation — mosquito cell culture (C6/36); research.
  • Rapid tests — NS1 + IgM/IgG combo card tests (SD Bioline).

Clinical Pearl

The most critical phase of dengue is around defervescence (day 3–7) — when fever drops but the patient may suddenly deteriorate into shock from capillary leak. The single most important monitoring parameter is haematocrit — a rise ≥20% from baseline indicates plasma leakage; a fall with stable haematocrit after fluid resuscitation indicates reabsorption (recovery phase). Platelet count alone does not predict severity — plasma leakage is the key determinant. Tourniquet test (Hess test) — inflate BP cuff to midway between systolic & diastolic for 5 min; >20 petechiae per square inch in 2.5 × 2.5 cm area = positive (suggests dengue). Treatment is supportive — meticulous fluid balance (isotonic crystalloid in critical phase; taper as recovery begins; avoid over-hydration which causes pulmonary oedema). Never give aspirin or NSAIDs (bleeding risk, Reye syndrome) — use paracetamol. Watch for warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy, mucosal bleeding) — these herald progression to severe dengue. WHO recommended fluid for DSS: isotonic crystalloids (Ringer's lactate or normal saline) bolus 10–20 mL/kg over 1 h, repeat if needed; if shock persists, add colloid (dextran, starch, albumin); switch back to crystalloid when stable. Live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia, CYD-TDV) — approved by WHO for seropositive individuals only (in seronegative, increases risk of severe dengue on subsequent infection due to ADE).

Introduction

Vibrio cholerae — Gram-negative, comma-shaped, facultatively anaerobic, polarly flagellated bacillus of family Vibrionaceae — is the causative agent of cholera. It is halophilic (salt-tolerant), alkaliphilic (grows at pH 8–9), and survives in brackish water, estuaries, and marine environments attached to plankton, copepods, and shellfish.

Classification (3 marks)

1. By Serogroup

  • V. cholerae has ~200 serogroups based on somatic O antigen.
  • O1 — causes classical epidemic cholera; further subdivided by serotype & biotype.
  • O139 Bengal — emerged 1992 in Chennai; causes epidemic cholera; capsule-positive; resistant to sulphamethoxazole-trimethoprim (SXT).
  • Non-O1 / Non-O139 (NAG — non-agglutinable vibrios) — usually cause sporadic watery diarrhoea or extraintestinal infections (wound, ear, sepsis); do not cause epidemics.

2. Serotypes of O1

  • Ogawa — A & B antigens; most common.
  • Inaba — A & C antigens.
  • Hikojima — A, B, C antigens; rare.

4. By Phage Type

  • Basu & Mukerjee phage typing — 5 phages classify El Tor into types 1–7; type 1 = classical El Tor; type 2 = Uber El Tor (Haiti variant — atypical El Tor that carries classical ctx gene).
  • Used in epidemiological tracking.

Pathogenesis (3 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Reservoir — humans (cases & asymptomatic carriers); aquatic environment (brackish water, estuaries — copepods, crustaceans).
  • Transmission — faecal-oral; contaminated water (primary); contaminated food (seafood, especially raw oysters; contaminated rice/millet).
  • Infective dose — high (10⁸–10¹¹ in fasting stomach; 10⁴–10⁶ if food buffers acid).
  • Incubation — 2 h to 5 days (typically 1–3 days).
  • Risk factors — hypochlorhydria (PPIs, antacids, gastrectomy), O blood group, malnutrition, immunocompromise, low gastric acidity.

2. Colonisation of Small Intestine

  1. Survival through stomach — acid-sensitive; high inoculum required; reaches alkaline small intestine (pH 8–9 optimum).
  2. Attachment
    • Flagellum — darting motility (chemotaxis toward mucus); characteristic "shooting star" movement on wet mount.
    • Mucinase — digests mucus barrier.
    • TCP (toxin-coregulated pilus) — type IV bundle-forming pilus; receptor for CTXφ bacteriophage (which carries cholera toxin gene); essential colonisation factor; basis of CVD 103-HgR vaccine.
    • Accessory colonisation factor (ACF).
    • Haemagglutinin/protease — breaks down mucin, fibronectin, lactoferrin; aids detachment & shedding.
  3. Vibrios do NOT invade — remain in lumen, attached to brush border.

3. Cholera Toxin (CT) Production

  • AB₅ enterotoxin; 84 kDa; encoded by ctxAB gene on CTXφ (lysogenic filamentous phage).
  • B pentamer (5 × 11.6 kDa) binds GM1 ganglioside on enterocyte brush border → endocytosis → retrograde transport through Golgi to ER.
  • A subunit (28 kDa) cleaved → A1 (active enzyme) + A2 (anchor).
  • A1 ADP-ribosylates arginine of Gsα (stimulatory G protein α-subunit) → locks Gsα in GTP-bound "ON" state → permanent activation of adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP.
  • cAMP activates PKA → phosphorylates CFTR chloride channel at apical membrane → massive Cl⁻ secretion into lumen; simultaneously inhibits NaCl absorption by Na/H exchanger.
  • Water follows osmotically → profuse secretory (rice-water) diarrhoea.
  • HCO₃⁻ & K⁺ also secreted → metabolic acidosis & hypokalaemia.
  • Loss of fluid & electrolytes → dehydration, hypovolaemic shock, AKI, death within hours if untreated.

4. Other Toxins

  • Zonula occludens toxin (Zot) — disrupts tight junctions → ↑intestinal permeability.
  • Accessory cholera enterotoxin (Ace) — increases fluid secretion.
  • RTX toxin — cytotoxic to cultured cells.
  • HlyA (haemolysin) — cytolytic.

5. Host Response

  • Vibrios do NOT invade mucosa → no inflammation → no fever, no blood/pus in stool, no faecal leucocytes.
  • Stool — "rice-water" (clear fluid flecked with mucus); alkaline; high K⁺, HCO₃⁻; high vibrio count (10⁷–10⁸/mL).
  • Immune response — secretory IgA against LPS & CTB; vibriocidal antibodies (IgM) protective; memory is serotype-specific.

Treatment

  • Rehydration is life-saving — ORS (WHO: Na 75, K 20, Cl 65, citrate 10, glucose 75 mmol/L) for mild–moderate; IV Ringer's lactate for severe (1 L in 30 min, then 100 mL/kg in 3 h for children).
  • Antibiotics — Doxycycline 300 mg single dose (adults); Azithromycin 500 mg × 3 d (children, pregnant); Ciprofloxacin 1 g single dose.
  • Zinc supplementation — children <5 yr (20 mg/day × 10–14 d).
  • Antimotility agents contraindicated.

Clinical Pearl

The cholera stool — "rice-water" — is pathognomonic: clear fluid flecked with mucus, like water in which rice has been washed. The patient is afebrile because the toxin is non-inflammatory; profound dehydration causes sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor ("washerwoman's hands"), absent tears & urine, weak pulse, hypotension, cold extremities, "cholera facies" with hoarse voice. Mortality in untreated severe cholera is 50–70%; with prompt rehydration <1%. The most common cause of incorrect IV fluid choice is using normal saline alone (lacks K⁺ and HCO₃⁻) — use Ringer's lactate (contains bicarbonate precursor). Tetracycline resistance is now widespread in El Tor strains; azithromycin is preferred first-line in India. Single-dose doxycycline 300 mg remains effective in most adults. For mass campaigns, WHO recommends single-dose OCV (oral cholera vaccine — Shanchol/Euvichol) in outbreak settings — protection lasts 6 months but interrupts transmission. India reports ~30,000–60,000 cholera cases annually (likely under-reported); outbreaks follow floods, religious gatherings (Kumbh Mela), and natural disasters.
